en: Govind Kaul: *Pradeśasaṃgraha* 1. The Mandala of Kashmir.
Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
In the first chapter (taraṅga) of the *Rājatarangiṇī* composed by Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa, verse 27 [states]: "Kaśmīrā;
its second name is Satīsaras. This is its etymological derivation (*nirukti*).
*Ka* means water; *śmīra* is derived from the root *smī*, meaning "to move," with the suffix *-ra* according to the *auṇādika* rules, such that it signifies "that from which [water] moves.
Thus, in the *Nīlamata*:
"From this region, water (*ka*) was removed by Balarāma (*halin*)."
Therefore, it shall become renowned throughout the entire world by the name Kaśmīra.
Furthermore, the meanings "moving" and "accomplishing" are also understood according to that very same opinion;
thus, even though the mandala was accomplished by Kaśyapa, its name is Kaśmīra.
This too is understood from the *Nīlamata* itself; for instance, who is designated as Prajāpati? Kaśyapa is Prajāpati.
"Therefore, by that name, the sacred site shall be known as Kaśmīra.
Regarding this word *kaśmīra*, its name in the Kāśmīrika language is *kaśīra*.
For this very reason, a man born in Kaśmīra has the name *kaśu*.
Furthermore, regarding the etymology of the word *kaśmīra*, there are many divergent views according to other authorities.
Thus, some who are learned in the traditions of the *Pāriṣeka-anuvāda* say it is *kaśyapamar*. According to their view, in the Kaśmīra language, the word *marpada* means "house."
And thus, it refers to the house of Kaśyapa.
Others, however, say that in former times there was a certain *rākṣasa* named Kaśū;
a certain Apsaras called Marpī (or Parīpā), who was under his control, also belonged to that very *rākṣasa*.
As those two wandered everywhere, they found a place to settle for their residence within this charming circle;
therefore, because it became famous by that very name, "Kaśmīra," this land attained renown throughout the entire world—thus they write in their own books.
However, there is no difference whatsoever between the pronunciation or usage of this name among both villagers and city-dwellers; so be it.
2. Nīlanāga: "Varanāgo vā" (verse 28, line 2). By Nīla, the lord of the *nāgas*, this *nāga* named Nīla was born as the son of the sage Kaśyapa.
In the region of Kaśmīra, who was the lord of the nāgas?

At the very time when his father Kaśyapa was establishing Kaśmīra, he was consecrated as the sovereign over those innumerable nāgas for the sake of training them in virtuous deeds and for the cessation of unwholesome conduct;
and it was in that very same settlement of Puragaṇa, which now bears the name Śrī Raṇavīrasiṃhapura, that this occurred.

There is a mountain known as Pīr Pañcāl, which serves as the boundary reckoned between the land of Kaśmīra and the land of Pañcanada. At a distance of half a krośa from that very mountain, along a path leading toward Kaśmīra, there lies a great, deep, octagonal reservoir of cool water, the dwelling place of the blue serpent.
This [place] has names such as Varanāga, Nīlanāga, Vīranāga, and so forth.

Among these, *varanāga* means an excellent nāga; *nīlanāga* refers to a nāga named Nīla, or a nāga possessing blue-colored water; and *vīranāga* means a nāga who is a hero (*vīra*). However, the villagers call this place by the name Vernāga.
Thus, even now there exists a village named Veranā;
furthermore, there is a similarity between Varanāga and Veranāga even in their pronunciation.
Some who follow the opinion of the Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā state that the name of the village is Vīrī, and they say that the serpent residing in the Vīrī district is named Vīrīnāga.

In this reservoir there are countless fish. Furthermore, on the western bank of this reservoir stands a large śāl tree planted by King Jyahaṃgīra of ancient times, in which a modern king carried out restoration and other works; here also is a garden established by that ancient king.
3. Kapaṭeśvaraḥ, verse 32, number 3: "The Lord of Umā in the form of wood.
This refers to Śiva, the husband and lord of Umā Pārvatī, who exists in the form of wood—that is, in the shape of wood.
For those men who perform that perfect touch of Śiva, the attainment of enjoyments occurs.

Formerly, for the sake of bestowing grace upon them, Śiva—who had been entreated by all the sages—consented to manifest his own form through a mere artifice. Then, having received such a boon from Śiva and returned, they were seen in this place as mere logs floating upon the water.
Therefore, this reservoir that had become a place of pilgrimage was given the name Kapaṭeśvara.
Even now, a large piece of wood is seen in this reservoir.

Furthermore, in the *Nīlamata*, during the description of the majesty of Kapaṭeśvara, it is said that when Śiva spoke to the sages, "I shall grant you a vision through a deception," the sages arrived at that very moment and [entered] into these waters.
The vision of Śiva in the form of wood was obtained;
therefore, the name of this place became Kapaṭeśvara.
Such is the story told at length.
The villagers call this place *Koṭyher* in the Kashmiri language;
for this very reason, the *puragaṇa* of Kuṭahāra also attained renown by this same name, in which this single village is still called by the name *Koṭyher* even today.
This *puragaṇa* is located four *krośas* below the previously mentioned *puragaṇa* of Śāhūbāda.
In this very place, known as Achyabala, there is a site dear to the minds of all people and renowned everywhere;
even the villagers continue to call this reservoir by the name Saṅkarṣaṇanāga.
4. Pāpasūdanatīrtha, verse 32, number 4: Pāpasūdana is within the group of tīrthas.
That which destroys—that is, annihilates—sins is called *pāpasūdana*, the sin-destroying tīrtha.
For those men who touch that sacred ford (tīrtha) and perform their ablutions there, the attainment of liberation occurs.
There, too, a great reservoir of water exists;
even in the Kashmiri language, the local villagers everywhere call this reservoir by the name "Pāpaharaṇa Nāga."
This reservoir is located in the Puragaṇa known as Khourpor in modern times, on the left side and within a short distance from the previously mentioned Kuṭahārapargana.
Therein also are two villages known as Sālīpāṃjamul;
situated right between those two is this reservoir called Pāpaharaṇanāga.
In this context, because the words *pāpasūdana* and *pāpaharaṇa* have identical meanings in Sanskrit, there is likewise no such distinction between them in the Kashmiri language.
This reservoir is quadrangular and is even smaller than the Nīlanāga. Occasionally, the Kashmiri name for the *vāriparṇī* plant is *muṅgol*.
Even when thus covered, it is still seen.
5. Trisandhyā Devī, verse 33, number 5: Sandhyā Devī.
She who is correctly meditated upon by the twice-born is Sandhyā.
And because that goddess is both radiant and playful, everyone calls this preeminent sacred site (tīrtha) by the name "Trisandhyā," which is renowned throughout the entire world.
This sacred site is situated on the slope of the mountain;
here there is a body of water that is circular in shape, narrow at the bottom and broad in its upper portion.

Furthermore, this [lake] is always dry during the spring season, yet it becomes full of water during the summer season; it is full of water three times by day and three times by night, and thus even when its water has dried up, it becomes full again.
That is to say, due to its instability, it alternates between possessing water and being devoid of water.
And so it has been stated in various scriptures, such as the Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā:
"Always dry in the rainy season, full in spring, and flowing turbulently in summer—the Sandhyā flows at three times; that Sandhyā bestows liberation.
Therefore, during the summer season in the month of Jyeṣṭha, the Sandhyā worship is performed just as it is done at dawn, midday, and evening.
In that very way, the procession of this best of holy places (tīrthavarasya) occurs like the twilight (sandhyā).
This reservoir is filled with rounded stones both in the middle and on its sides.

At the time when the water, having been offered during the twilight rite, begins to dry up, at that very moment mice emerge from those stone apertures and cast [offerings] into the reservoir for the sake of worship.
They eat unbroken grains and other such offerings.
Near this best of holy places (tīrtha), there are seven reservoirs belonging to the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis);
from them, even a single small stream flows forth.
The Alpanadī flows below this most excellent mountain tīrtha.
At the time of performing the twilight rites, the water from the tīrtha emerges from its reservoir and falls into the middle of the river's current;
there, at that confluence-tīrtha, one performs ritual bathing and other rites.

This reservoir is located near the Bhṛṅgipura group of villages mentioned previously, which are situated close to the Kuṭahārapura group; there is a village named Divalgā situated in its midst, which is well-known.
Both the villagers and the Kashmiris call this sacred site by the name Sundabhrār.
In that regard, *bhrār* is the name for a goddess in the Kashmiri language;
therefore, *Sundabhrār* means "the beautiful goddess. For this group of villages (*puragaṇa*) and the village of Bhṛṅga, the term *divalgon* is used by the villagers in their speech.
Below this village, there are two villages known as Bihū and Jalan-gām.
At the head of this excellent tīrtha, there stands a single tree that serves as a landmark, resembling a *pippala* (peepul) tree.
At the time of performing the twilight rituals, when the water appears, the water comes forth even upon the offering of flowers, unbroken rice grains, food oblations, and other such items.
At that time, everyone performs their bathing and other rites by drawing water directly from the reservoir itself.

Then, at the time for performing the second twilight ritual (saṃdhyā), when people remain waiting with disciplined composure, the water emerges outside as before, merges with the waters of the confluence (saṃgama), and thus their bathing and other rites are accomplished.

Whenever any royal officers bearing staffs, along with swords and other weapons, approach the bank of this reservoir at the time of performing their twilight rites in an impure and undisciplined manner, the water disappears from sight upon seeing those who are both impure and undisciplined.
Therefore, this excellent holy site is in every way marvelous, venerable, and worthy of worship; it is also the most renowned in this land.
For this very reason,
Kalhaṇa’s statement that "the vision [of the king] follows the positive and negative concomitance of merits and demerits" appears to be true, since only those possessing merit obtain his audience.
But sinners, even having gone there, return without having seen [the deity].
6. Svayambhūḥ Agniḥ (Verse 34, No. 6): *Svayambhūḥ*.
He who is the consumer of oblations (*hutabhuk*) by himself alone, and not one who is ignited by anyone else, is *svayambhūḥ*.
Such is this fire, the consumer of oblations (*hutabhuj*).

Regarding the description of its majesty, it is written that in ancient times, at the request of sages and devotees, Śiva manifested his own form as Kālāgnirudra in this very place. Thus it has been recorded.
In all these cases, there exists a desert land called *Uḍar* in the language known as Hindī, and also in the Kāśmīrī language;
that very same land is observed in many places to have reached a state of ripeness and to be a source of heat.
Therefore, it is understood that this fire does not always emerge from only a single location.
However, at one time it arises in one place, at another time in another, and sometimes it arises here from that very source.
And the elders say: "This fire always manifests in this very location after a period of more than twelve years, or even longer.
Here, travelers arrive, purify their own goods with care, and [place] them in those very vessels according to their respective measures.

Having poured rice and water into a hollow dug in the ground scraped with wood, they placed those food vessels upon that very heated ground for half a muhūrta; then, just as they were removing the respective vessels from the pits,
they saw that the food in those vessels was perfectly cooked and, moreover, superior to the food being cooked by everyone else over a fire of fuel and such.

Then those travelers perform the *śrāddha* and other rites for their ancestors with that very food, preceded by the offering of *piṇḍas*, according to their desire and according to the prescribed rules.
Those who desire to perform the *homa* ritual, however, having scattered dry wood on all sides upon that same heated ground, kindle a flame with clarified butter and other substances;
they then perform the *homa* within those very flames according to the procedure taught in their own *gṛhya-sūtra*. Therefore...
Even the statement of Kalhaṇa, "He receives the oblation with the mouths of his flaming arms," and so forth, is consistent;
for this fire, possessing greater flames than the fire being ignited, receives the oblation.
The region of ground where this fire has manifested is perceived as being extremely hot even by the touch of the hands and other limbs.
Both villagers and city-dwellers call this place by its own name, which is renowned throughout the entire world.
This site is located within the group of towns known as Macchepor, situated in the kingdom of Krama.
At this time, the villagers call this place Kamrāj, which is part of the Puragaṇa district of Kramarājya, and they say it is Tapaymacchyapūr.
They are seen saying that for whichever village this fire belongs to, it is the *niccahaum* of that village.
Near this village of Nicyahaum, there are also two other villages.
In this regard, the villagers themselves say that one village situated near Nicyahaum is called Rājypaur, while another village situated below it is called Jacyalaur;
in these two villages, people designated by the term *rājya* live as *mlecchas*.
This village of Nicyahaum is a marvel of this fire, which from the site of Sūryapura has acquired the modern name Sopor through the pronunciation of the villagers.
At a distance of twenty *krośas* from that place there is a region;

although in this village there is only desert land at places scorched by fire and the like, nevertheless, in the fields of grain on both sides near it, the production of crops and so forth certainly occurs.
7. Haṃsavāgīśvarī, also known by the alternative name Bheḍā Devī, verse 35, number 7: Sarasvatī in the form of a swan;
she is the Goddess who destroys the darkness characterized by ignorance (avidyā), thus she is the "Haṃsa," the Supreme Self (paramātman).
That is to say, her form is that very power.

Such is Sarasvatī, the goddess presiding over speech, whose name is Vāgīśvarī; this Sarasvatī in the form of a *haṃsa* is seen by all upon the peak—that is, the summit—of the mountain named Bheḍā, which is rendered exceedingly pure by the manifestation of the river named Bhṛṅgī.
On this mountain there is a lake;
that very lake exists as the abode of Haṃsavāgīśvarī. The river that flows through the district of the city called Bhṛṅga flows at the foot of the aforementioned mountain known as Bhṛṅgī.
The villagers, however, call the Puragaṇa by the name "Bhṛṅga," and they also refer to the village situated at the foot of Bheḍa Hill as "Bhiḍar" using the very word "Bheḍa.
Modern inhabitants living in that village, on the other hand, say that the lake located on Bheḍa Hill is named Kātyāyanī-Ṭāḍāga.
In that regard, it refers to the lake— that is, the pond— of the goddess Kātyāyanī, who is none other than Haṃsavāgīśvarī.
And there are those who, due to the corruption of Apabhraṃśa, call the name of this Kātyāyanī-taḍāga "Kāntrāg."

Regarding that, as for "whom," it refers to Kātyāyanī; previously, there was a lake on that mountain, and at the summit of the mountain, a reservoir exists, while at its foot, rivers also flow. Therefore, the Goddess herself [resides] on the peak of Bheḍagiri, pure with the source of the Gaṅgā.
The statement of Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa— that Sarasvatī is seen within a lake in the form of a swan— is also consistent with this fact:
in this village called Bhiḍara, there is a stone image of the Goddess situated in the midst of the waters of this river.

The local villagers, regarding her as Bheḍadevī herself, invoke and worship her under the name "Bheḍadevī. In the midst of this Puragaṇa known as Bhṛṅga, there flows a river which, being designated by the word "Bhṛṅga," is named Bhṛṅgī; it is this very river that Kalhaṇa has referred to by the name Gaṅgā in his own work.
Furthermore, it is precisely from the name of the goddess Bhedādevī that the village’s name became Bhiḍar.
In reality, however, the lake situated on the mountain in the village of Bhiḍar is the abode of Haṃsavāgīśvarī;
and the river called Bhṛṅgī, which flows below the mountain, also originates from that very mountain.
According to the belief of the villagers, whichever stone image exists within that water is Bheḍādevī;
the water of this lake remains always of one and the same form, never increasing nor ever decreasing.
Its water is highly digestive, cooling, and sweet.
8. Nandikṣetra, Verse 36, Number 8: In Nandikṣetra;
he who gladdens—that is, causes all his devotees to rejoice—is Nandī, Śiva.
That sacred field (*kṣetra*) which is his *tīrtha* is Nandikṣetra.
Alternatively, Nandikṣetra is that very place which has become a *tīrtha* for the sake of propitiating the attendant (*anucara*) of Śiva named Nandin, who is a leader among the *gaṇas*.

It is said that in ancient times, on the mountain called Hara-mukuṭa, while Pārvatī was staying in seclusion, her own attendant and chief of the *gaṇas*, named Nandin, was stationed by her at the base of that mountain in a region known as Dhāra.
From that time onward, Nandikṣetra was established there.

Accordingly, in the Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā, during the description of the majesty of the pilgrimage to the Gaṅgā on Hara’s crown, it is said that once Pārvatī beheld the Gaṅgā gushing forth from the matted-hair crown (jaṭāmukuṭa) known as Kaparda, which rested upon Śiva’s head.

Then, seeing her as a co-wife of Śiva’s beloved, she—out of jealousy toward her rival and with eyes crooked and blinded by rage—said to Śiva, "Release this co-wife of mine. Although she was entreated many times by Śiva, Pārvatī maintained a persistent insistence, saying, "If I am your most beloved, then you must certainly abandon her."

Furthermore, at the very moment that Śiva, overcome by devotion to Pārvatī, released Gaṅgā from his own crest-jewel of matted hair, the name "Haramukuṭagaṅgā" was bestowed upon that Gaṅgā; for since Gaṅgā emerged from the crest of Hara— Śiva— she is called Haramukuṭagaṅgā.
Alternatively, because she fell from Hara’s crown to the ground due to her extreme restlessness, she is called the "Crown-Gaṅgā" (Mukuṭagaṅgā).
Furthermore, Śiva made this request to Pārvatī with great honor:
"O Goddess, this Gaṅgā who was released from my head by your command, I shall bear her once again"—such was Śiva's [request].
Upon hearing these words, the Goddess, overcome with extreme anger, abandoned Śiva and ascended Mount Hara-mukuṭa, her own dwelling place, in order to manifest her pride.

At the time of her ascent, she commanded Nandin, the chief attendant of Śiva and guardian of that mountain: "O Nandin, I shall remain here on the mountain peak alone for some time to maintain my secret."
"Therefore, standing here at the entrance of this mountain, you must act in such a way that no one else sees me while I am staying in private.
Furthermore, if anyone should come desiring to enter my presence, you must not grant entry to anyone at all.
Having received such an order from Śiva, Nandin remained as motionless as a stone, blocking the entrance; at that very moment, Śiva too, searching for the Goddess everywhere—
He reached the foot of Mount Haramukuṭa.

There, although Śiva saw his attendant Nandin standing as motionless as a rock, he was intent on entering into the presence of the Goddess; yet, just as he was about to begin the ascent of the mountain, Nandin informed him that the Goddess, who was staying in private, had not given permission for him to ascend there.

Having said, "Therefore, you must not ascend," he was blocked and forbidden. Then, although Śiva himself addressed Nandin many times, as long as he saw him not wavering even slightly from his own obstinacy, the god, his eyes crooked with extreme anger, cursed him thus: "O fool, because you [have obstructed] me on this mountain..."

"And since you even despise the Lord of the Goddess, therefore, from this day forward, on the lower part of this mountain, you shall become one of dull intellect, with the form of matted hair, and extremely hard due to my shadow.
(In this passage, because the letters *la* and *ḍa* are identical in the Sanskrit language, they share the same meaning.)
"You shall become water.

Hearing this fire of a curse issuing from the lotus-face of Śiva, Nandin also thought in his mind: "Aha! How is it that he obeys the command of Śivā, who is half of Śiva? Why has this Śiva, without reflection, given this curse to her in vain?"
Reflecting on this, he resolved to curse his own master and said:

"Since you have uttered a curse against me without due deliberation, even though I was under another's control, therefore, from this day forward, you too shall become a personification of Death (Kāla) right here near my pool by virtue of my curse;
that is to say, you shall become a body of water containing the waters of Death."

Therefore, from that very time onwards, two reservoirs situated near Mount Hara-mukuṭa became the Pāvaka-tīrthas through the granting of a boon by Śiva. Of these, one is named Nandikṣetra and the other is named Kālakṣetra;
even in the present day, this pair of reservoirs is so called.
The White Water and the Black Water, indicated by these very names, come within the range of vision of travelers;
however,
in the sacred field of Nandi, they are offered by sky-dwellers in the temple of Surāvāsa.
Even today, it is there that drops of sandalwood paste used for worship are still manifested.

Thus, that which was written by Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa in his own book does not accord with anything at all—such as the sight of drops of sandalwood paste—in the present day due to the absence of palaces and other such structures.

Therefore, it is known that all of this must indeed have existed in ancient times; furthermore, the two names of these aforementioned pairs of water-reservoirs, *Nund* and *Kol*, are spoken by everyone in the vernacular language of the Kashmiri villagers.
These two holy sites (tīrtha) are situated on the borderland of the community of the city named Laharā, in the vicinity of the Hara-mukuṭa-Gaṅgā.
On the route for the pilgrimage to the Hara-mukuṭa-Gaṅgā, one first beholds these very two holy sites.
Thereafter, pilgrims arrive at the banks of the Mukuṭagaṅgā.
This group of villages is called Lārpargaṇa in the local dialect, and the name of the Mukuṭagaṅgā is Gaṅgabal;
for in the Kāśmīrī language, *bal* is the term used for a place-name.
Therefore, *gaṅgābala* means, in effect, the location of the Gaṅgā.
During this pilgrimage to the Gaṅgā on Hara’s crown, there is a village called Nunar situated seven *krośas* distant from the city of Kashmir.
Pilgrims arrive there on the first day and, on the second day, they reach the village of Rāmarādhan by following the very path that leads to the river known by the name Karaṅkanadī.
As far as this village of Rāmarādhaṅga, the fields of grain and other crops, as well as the trees situated within the village, are visible in every way;
starting from this place, however, there are only mountains everywhere.
Among those foremost of mountains is the one named Bharata, which, according to the opinion of the villagers, is called Bharuth.
Having ascended it, travelers proceed;
from this very place onward, no village or such can be found until reaching the Gaṅgā at Hara’s crown.
Even the trees here are seen everywhere to be merely wild forest trees.
From Mount Bharata up to the crown of Śiva’s head, nowhere can such trees be found from which fuel might be taken for the purpose of cooking food and the like.
However, there is a single piece of wood shaped like a creeper that, while still moist, burns at that very moment once it has been uprooted.
That wood is known by the name *vānarendhana* (monkey-fuel).
And so Kalhaṇa says: "Even when in contact with fire, ordinary wood-fuel does not burn because it lacks potency;

yet this *kāṣṭhabheda* (fire-stone), even though devoid of flames, certainly accomplishes actions such as cooking. Regarding its name, it is called *viṭhur*, *viṭhar*, or *kāṭh* in the speech of the villagers."
9. Śāradā Devī, Verse No. 9: Regarding Śāradā Devī, here is the etymological derivation of the term *śāradā*:
she who cuts (*dyati*) or shatters (*khaṇḍayati*) the net (*jāla*) of arrows (*śara*), that is, the multitude of shafts, directed at the Daityas, is Śāradā.
Alternatively, according to the dictionary (*kośa*) which states that *śāra* means "wind" or "variegated" in three senses,
it is that which cuts— that is, destroys— the wind of the form of illusion (*māyārūpa*).
Furthermore:
She is she who bestows *śāra*—that is, variegated, manifold knowledge pertaining to the sciences (*śāstra*) as well as the arts (*śilpa*) and so forth;
furthermore, through the identity of the letters *śa* and *sa*, she is both *Śāradā* and *Sāradā*.
In that regard, she is *Sāradā* because she bestows *sāra*—meaning strength, fitness, knowledge, boons, and the like—and is supreme.
Those people who behold such a goddess Śāradā—
that is, those who undertake the pilgrimage to Śāradā—
will certainly, by her grace, become served by poets.
Even by poets who are always being honored,
they attain the speech that is the refined Sanskrit language in its manifest form (*vaikharī*);
through the grace of the boon of Śāradā, they become poets endowed with poetic power, skilled in the work of poetry.
Furthermore,
those who set out on a pilgrimage to that sacred site necessarily reach the river named Madhumatī as well;
that is to say, there is also a famous river called Madhumatī situated along the route of that pilgrimage.
Therefore, they also obtain that [river] on the middle path; hence,
Kalhaṇa’s statement that "the river Taraṅgiṇī and the honeyed speech frequented by poets," and so forth, is most appropriate.
By virtue of taking refuge in this very Goddess Śāradā, some people also call this land of Kaśmīra by the name Śāradāpīṭha.
In that regard, since the etymology is "the seat (pīṭha) of Śāradā," it is indeed correct to say that this region, which serves as the abode of Śāradā, is denoted by the term Śāradāpīṭha.
Here, at the site of Goddess Śāradā, there is a body of water in the shape of a pool (kuṇḍa).
Upon it lies a single large stone by which that entire pool is concealed, yet it remains visible in every respect. Here,
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, a pilgrimage is performed by pilgrims.
Furthermore, it is here that the entire sequence of ritual acts, beginning with the sowing of seeds and including the *śrāddha* and *homa*, is accomplished.
From the city of Kaśmīra, the Śāradā-tīrtha is reached in eight stages known as *paḍāv*.
Along the way, travelers must entirely traverse a difficult path that is exceedingly watery.
This site of Śāradā exists entirely beyond the entire mandala of the Kramarājya, situated in the place known as Drau, which lies at its forefront.
In the Kashmiri language, they call this site of Śāradā by the name Śārad.
This district of Draupura has ancient connections with many regions situated on the borderlands of Kashmir, such as Karaṇāva, Mujapharābād, Gilgit, and others.
The people residing in this place are known by the name Gujjers;
they are seen speaking the language spoken in the Pañcanada region. For those traveling on a pilgrimage to this place, there are two routes for travel.
10. *Cakradharaḥ*, verse 38, number 10: *cakrabhṛt*. He who bears (*bibharti*) or holds (*dhārayati*) the discus (*cakra*) is the discus-bearer (*cakrabhṛt*), namely Viṣṇu.
In this context, because the roots *bhṛ* and *bhr̥ṅ* are identical in meaning— namely, "to bear"— *cakrabhṛt* (bearer of the discus) is indeed the same as *cakradhara* (holder of the discus).

Long ago, it is said, when the entire earth was rendered unstable and oppressed by various Daityas who caused manifold disturbances— having become intoxicated by boons obtained through the power of their asceticism, and thus burdening the world with their afflictions— at that very time...
Having approached the gods, she said while weeping:
"O gods, these Daityas, arrogant because of the boon they have received, are oppressing me in every way; what shall I do?
Or how shall I endure this?"

Then those gods, having heard the piteous lamentation of that goddess Earth and having consoled her with words that inspired confidence, themselves became agitated; and in great haste, they went together with that goddess Earth for refuge to the Blessed Viṣṇu, the protector of the entire world.
Having arrived there, those gods, after praising that Lord with many meaningful hymns, spoke of their desire for his welcome:
"O Lord, we all, as well as this earth, being oppressed by wicked Daityas, have now come to you, O Blessed One, for refuge because of our extreme distress.
Therefore, you ought to ordain the destruction of the Daityas so that we may attain peace along with this Goddess."
Then, having heard what was desired by the gods, the Blessed One placed those gods and that Earth-goddess before him and went to the world of Śiva for the purpose of propitiating Śiva.

There, the Blessed One, together with those gods, propitiated Śiva—who was none other than his own form—through hymns of praise and other appropriate forms of worship; and having reported the purpose of his arrival to Śiva, he received from him, who was thus duly gratified, [the desired boon].
At that very moment, he obtained the discus named Sudarśana, the destroyer of the hosts of Daityas.
From that time forward, Viṣṇu, bearing that discus, began the ritual procedure for slaying the Daityas stationed everywhere.
For this very reason, in order to slay the Daityas residing in Kaśmīra, Viṣṇu took up his station here in the region situated near Vijayeśvara.
Because he resorted to that very place previously mentioned as the abode of Cakradhara, the name "Cakradhara" became established for him.
However, the villagers now call that Cakradhara by the name "Cakadhar" in the Kaśmīrī language.
And the modern name of that place near Vijayeśvara where this Cakadhar resides is "Vijyabhror."

This [region] is Vijyabhrū, and this Cakradhara is likewise situated within the Dakṣiṇapārśva Puragaṇa, which is currently known by the name Dacchunporpargaṇa according to the opinion of the villagers; it exists right in the middle of that.

Here there is a river named Lambodarī, which is now called Lidar in the vernacular of the villagers; the left and right banks of that very river are what are designated as the Left Side (Vāmapārśva) and the Right Side (Dakṣiṇapārśva).

In that place, according to the Kashmiri language, the two names for the left flank are *khourporpargaṇa* and for the right flank *dacchunporpargaṇa*. Near this Cakadhara is another village whose name is *Simathana*;
that too exists here. Nowadays, Cakadhara appears like a small mountain.
This region called Cakradhara is situated on the bank on the southern side of the river Vitastā.
Some say that there is a great ritual site (mahāvidhi) here, beneath Cakradhara.
In former times, whoever traveled back and forth along that path invariably and always received coins such as *dīnāras*— which are synonymous with ancient *rūpakas*— in accordance with the tradition.

Even in the present age, any man who is extremely destitute resorts to this Daitya with great devotion, regarding this very region as being presided over by Cakradhara himself, out of hope for wealth.
He goes;
he too will certainly obtain some wealth or other.
This region is situated fourteen *krośas* distant to the east of the city of Kaśmīra.
For those nāgas coming from Ananta who arrive at the city of Kaśmīra, this region first comes into their field of vision after they have already traversed three *krośas*;
it is situated at a distance of only one *krośa* from Vijayeśvara.
On the ground where this Cakradhara stands, there have long been trees belonging even to Kaśmīra—so be it.

11. Vijayeśvaraḥ (Vijayeśa), verse number 38: He who prevails (*jayati*) with supreme excellence (*sarvotkarṣeṇa*) above all hosts of gods (*devagaṇeṣu*) is *vijaya*. He who possesses that [quality] is *vijayeśa*. 11. Vijayeśvaraḥ. Verse 38: *Vijayeśa*. He who especially (*viśeṣeṇa*) triumphs (*jayati*) and exists in a state of preeminence over all the hosts of deities is *Vijaya*. He who possesses that [quality] is *Vijayeśa*. 11. Vijayeśvaraḥ. Verse 38: *Vijayeśa*. He who especially
Alternatively, he who conquers or overcomes various hosts such as the Daityas is Vijaya. He is also Īśa; he who rules and bestows sovereignty is Īśa.
Vijaya himself is Īśa, thus he is Vijayeśa.
The image of Śiva situated in this region is designated by the term Vijayeśa, because the form of Śiva alone is everywhere recited as being denoted by the word "Īśa.
It is inferred that this region called Vijayeśvara has been most widely known by this very name for an exceedingly long time,
since only those who perform tasks such as restoration (jīrṇoddhāra) are found here.
However, the name of the author is generally not established directly;
for even the scholar Kalhaṇa writes in the fifth verse, numbered one hundred and one, of the first book of his own *Rājatarangiṇī*, as follows: Thus it is said: [text of the verse]... Thus indeed.
Having had the dilapidated plaster wall of Śrī Vijayeśa removed,
he caused a stone wall to be constructed by Niṣkalmaṣa.

The meaning is "by King Aśoka. Here, by both the mention of the removal of the plastered wall (*sudhāmaya-prākāra*) and the mention of the construction of the stone wall (*aśmamaya-prākāra*), it is understood that this region was already in existence previously, and thus its extreme antiquity is established.

In the *Pāriśeṣaka* manuscripts, some state that this region called Vijayeśvara was established by King Surendra— who lived even earlier than King Aśoka— while others claim it was built by Queen Īśānadevī, the consort of King Jalaukas, who ruled the land after Kings Surendra and Aśoka. Furthermore, certain [authors] are seen writing in their own books that the original construction of the site was performed by King Aśoka himself.
However, among these three views, none appears to be the most consistent or correct.

In that regard, in the description of King Surendra in the ninety-first verse of the first chapter of the *Rājatarangiṇī*, although his victory over Vijayeśvara is described, even the name of Vijayeśvara does not appear;
therefore, the claim that this [temple] was established by Surendra is also untenable.

As for those who claim that this region was established by the queen known as Īśānadevī, the consort of King Jalauka, [one finds] that in the account of King Jalauka’s life described in the first book (Prathamataraṅga) of the *Rājatarangiṇī*, starting from the 107th verse, and even within the account of that aforementioned queen included therein, the name Vijayeśvara is not found anywhere.
Therefore, that too appears entirely inconsistent.

As for those who, considering Aśokarāja alone to be the restorer of Vijayeśvara, write in their own books that Aśoka himself was the restorer of Vijayeśvara and so forth— they are like those who, having demolished a dilapidated wall made of plaster, proceed to construct a new wall made of stone.
Having obtained [the text] from the *Rājatarangiṇī* itself and knowing that he personally carried out the work of its restoration and so forth, they write accordingly;
therefore, even that appears to them as something unexamined,
for there is a great difference between the editor and the one who performed the restoration.

In fact, since the name of Vijayeśvara is not seen at all even at the beginning of the *Rājatarangiṇī*, it is understood that even the scholar Kalhaṇa did not personally know the builder of this site; for he did not mention any such account even while describing the line of kings prior to King Aśoka. Therefore, its extreme antiquity is established.
It appears clearly as such.
Here, on the left side of the Vitastā river, which is visible at the point where the path from Anantanāga arrives, stands this very temple known as Vijayeśvara;
so say the elders.

It was said that in this region there had always stood a stone-built temple dedicated to the deity Mandira; however, the stone structure currently visible at this time was built by King Śrī Raṇavīrasiṃha— who had attained a high station in the celestial realm and was the sovereign of many lands such as Kaśmīra and Jambū— for many years.
It was acquired by expending a thousand coins with great hardship and immense effort.
Now there is a statue of Śiva in this temple;
for the maintenance of its worship and other rites, the king has established a village under the designation of an *agrahāra*, and another has been set aside for the honoring of guests.

The villagers, however, understanding this temple to have been built by Haricandra, call it by its name in their own Kashmiri language, *Haricandrājan mandir*, and they also give the names *Haricandrājun* and *Yārabal* to the water descending from the riverbank and to the flight of stairs, respectively.
In this context, the meaning is that the first name refers to the temple built by Haricandra,
while the second name means this flight of stairs was constructed by Haricandra;
for in the Kashmiri language, all flights of stairs are designated by the word *yārabal*.
In that regard, in the Kashmiri language, the word for "friend" is *yār*.
For those very friends, *bal* means "place," because in the land of Kashmir, everyone resorts to the riverbank at the very hour of dawn for bathing;
therefore, those who are friends with one another gather there.

For this very reason, the name *Yārabal* came to belong to this riverbank. Here, having gone only a few paces above Vijayeśvara, there are many trees known in the vernacular as *cinār*, which in the scholarly language (*saṃskṛtabhāṣā*) are designated by the term *chāyāvṛkṣa*.

Likewise, on the opposite bank facing Vijayeśvara along the Vitastā, there are also many trees of the aforementioned kind. People say that these two places, surrounded by groves of trees, were the two pleasure gardens of an ancient king.
The name of these two gardens, as spoken by the villagers, is Pādaśāhyabāg.
According to his opinion, this region is named Vijyabhroḥ;
here, very near Vijayeśvara, there is also a ferry for crossing from one bank of the river to the other,
which they call Kadal of Vijyabhroḥ.
In this aforementioned parkland, the remains of structures built by kings in ancient times, such as those of Aikṣvāka and others, are still clearly visible today; may there be peace.
12. Ādikeśavaḥ, verse number 38: Regarding Ādikeśava, this is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of Keśava.
He who pervades Ka (Brahmā), Aṃ (Viṣṇu), and Īśa (Śiva) by means of his own luminosity, and who covers them while they are being manifested within him—he is Keśava.

And thus, He who exists even at the beginning of the creation and so forth of this entire world is Ādikeśava; by implication, he is the performer of such acts as the creation, preservation, and destruction of the world. That very first, eternal Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, is the one designated by the term Ādikeśava.
Since this very form of the Blessed Viṣṇu is the one that remains here today among all the various forms of deities situated within this Kaśmīra maṇḍala,
it has consequently become designated by the term *Ādikeśava*.
Because of the presence of this very Ādikeśava, the name *Ādyāvanī* became attached to this group of cities as well.
In this context, "Ādyāvanī" means that which exists at the beginning, namely the earth (*bhūmi*).
Because of the presence of Ādikeśava, this very earth has become the foremost among all lands and the locus of preeminence; for this reason, she is known as "Ādyāvanī.
According to the view of some, however, when this earth was formerly in the state of the Satī lake, and was entirely overflowing with water on all sides—

This region was then entirely covered by lakes that were constantly replenished by the excellence of the local qualities of being river-fed, characterized by eddies, the breaking of whirlpools, and various transformations of the water; this occurred at the time when, through the grace of the hosts of gods satisfied by the power of the asceticism of the sage Kaśyapa,
the land manifested its nature as earth for the purpose of establishing settlements and districts for the habitation of people.
"In this very place, the primordial earth (ādyāvanī) is that which has become the object of perception as 'earth' (bhūmitva).
For this very reason, this group of cities is designated as 'the primordial earth' (ādyāvanī), and so forth.
Regarding that, the word *ādyāvanī* means "that earth which exists at the beginning" (*ādau bhavā yā sā cāsau bhūmiḥ*), i.e., the primordial earth (*ādyabhūmi*).
And even today, in this district of Avinipura, there exists a single reservoir known by this name, whose form as designated by the term *Keśava* appears now in this manner:
it is described as being broad in its upper portion and contracted in its lower portion.
This reservoir, like the previously described reservoir of the goddess Sandhyā, is circular in shape.
The villagers, however, now say that the image of Ādikeśava belonging to this village is located at a reservoir called Phrasal in that village;
furthermore, they call the district (puragaṇa) in which this village is situated by the name Āḍvin.
This reservoir also has a name well-known in their language: Keśavanāg.
In this context, "Nāga" refers to a reservoir of water belonging to this very Keśava, namely Ādikeśava;
for in the land of Kaśmīra, all reservoirs of water whatsoever are designated by the term "nāga.
Furthermore, near this village known as Phrasal, there is yet another village.
Its name is Ārvañ;

therefore, some villagers pronounce the name as a compound, "Phrasal-ārvañ. The group of Āḍvin-puragas who serve as the inhabitants of this reservoir reside on a tract of land situated below the Devasarpu-ragaṇa.
13. Īśānaḥ, verse number 38: Īśāna. He who rules over the entire world and exercises sovereignty is Īśāna.

The one who is the lord of all the hosts of gods, who dwells in the world, who seeks the perfection of rice and sovereignty, and who is Śiva—the master of all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and all prosperities (*bhūti*)—is designated by the term *Īśāna*. The meaning is that this form of Śiva is located in the region described as a synonym for both the terms *Śiva* and *Īśāna*. Alternatively, he is Sandhimat, as described in the second book of the *Rājatarangiṇī* composed by the scholar Kalhaṇa.

The preceptor of the king named Ceta—who, by his grace, caused that deceased king Sandhimati to regain his life—is indeed the one named Īśāna; because of that name, this image of Śiva located here has come to be designated by the term "Īśāna.
And so it is stated in the thirty-seventh verse of the second book of Kalhaṇa’s *Rājatarangiṇī*:
Having established Sandhīśvara in the cremation ground for the ancestors where his body was joined together,
he fashioned Hara as Īśeśvara under the name of his guru, Īśāna.
Although he was known by the name Īśeśvara, he attained fame through the very name of that Īśāna;
for even if this region had already been exceedingly pure and possessed of great majesty due to the manifestation of Śiva’s form prior to the time of Īśāna, nevertheless,
it became so entirely [famous] by virtue of the manifestation of the most wonderful deeds of Īśāna alone.
Fame has been achieved.

Here, beginning from the sixty-fifth verse in this second wave, it is described that this very person named Sandhimati was formerly the minister of King Vijaya’s son, the one called Jayendra; he was a disciple of Īśāna and the most excellent among the wise.

Then the courtiers spoke to the king—who was like an elephant in rut with flapping ears—saying, "This minister Sandhimati is truly extraordinary and possesses immense power; therefore, you must certainly take precautions against him regarding the seizure of the kingdom and other such matters.
For this very reason, the king, having been deceived by him, conceived a sense of enmity toward that wise minister and seized hold of him with great anger.

Then, that king— his affection for the minister forgotten due to their enmity— first forbade him from entering his own assembly hall and subsequently stripped him of all his possessions, thereby reducing the minister to lifelong poverty.

Even though he had fallen into such a miserable state, the minister did not perceive his own ruin in state affairs as a cause for distress, because he had obtained the opportunity to perform the auspicious worship of Śiva without any obstacles.
Then, due to the power of the destined event, this very prophecy—that the kingdom would belong to Sandhimati alone—suddenly became renowned in every house.
And so it is said in the seventy-fourth verse of the second chapter:
"Then, by the greatness of the destined event, [the fame] spread from house to house."
"The kingdom shall belong to Sandhimat"—even though this voice was unheard, Sarasvatī spoke it.

Then, upon hearing such a voice as previously described, the king suddenly realized that since no such voice had ever circulated before, it must certainly have been instigated by a god or some other supernatural being; and having conceived a great fear, he cast that minister into prison.

There, ten years passed for him as his feet were tormented by fierce shackles and he consequently reached a state of emaciation. Those very ten years became the limit of the remainder of the life of King Jayendra, the lord Sandhimati; meanwhile, he was tormented by the affliction of a fatal disease and by the excessive suffering caused by anxiety over his mother and his son, and thus, desiring death, he remained within.
Thus he fell into great torment.

Being scorched day and night by that fire of the minister’s magical incantation, which blazed incessantly, the king could think of no remedy for his fate other than the execution of that minister. Alas! Men who consider themselves wise employ whatever means possible to conceal a future event; yet that very same means, thwarted by destiny, serves to bring about that very event.
Just as fate, by its own command, desires to bestow incomparable power upon even a tiny spark of fire situated within a heap of wood, so too,
when it is about to bestow great power upon that aforementioned spark, anyone who—
unaware of the force of destiny— seeks to extinguish it, finds that very destiny [acting] upon a jar of ghee mixed with ghee melted by heat.
He created the illusion of a water-jar.
Then, at the very moment the king commanded the executioners to carry out the execution for the sake of killing the minister, Sandhimati was impaled upon a stake by them and killed.
When that minister had been transfixed on the stake, first the dart of suffering born of the minister's anxiety emerged from that king.

Afterwards, even his life departed. Then, having heard of the death of his own disciple who had been struck down in such a manner, the heart of his teacher, named Īśāna—who though self-controlled was not immune to grief—became inwardly tormented. Thereupon, for the sake of performing the funeral rites for that disciplined disciple at the time of his passing, Īśāna went to that very cremation ground where the death of the one who had formed a connection with the earth had occurred.

There, Īśāna, having pinned his own disciple to that very base of the stake, saw him reduced to mere bones, with the fragments of bone below being forcibly dragged away by jackals. Upon seeing him, overcome with great and intense grief, he cried out, "Alas, my child! I live only to see you in such a state! And restraining the howling jackal from the skeleton impaled on that stake, he led him away.
Then, just as that lord was about to perform the final customary consecration, he recited this verse inscribed by fate upon the forehead of his own disciple:
"Poverty for as long as one lives; ten years of imprisonment."
Death shall come upon the back of the spear, and thereafter there will be sovereignty.
Thus it was said.

Consequently, that teacher, having understood the meaning of these three lines of the verse exactly as they were stated, became filled with curiosity regarding the meaning of the fourth line—which he felt compelled to see—and reflected in his mind: "How indeed will this come to pass?"

Then, having reflected upon that power of inconceivable majesty by which Arjuna, Parikṣit, Kaca, and others, though previously dead, had attained life once more— that power which accomplishes the impossible— he praised the Lord, who is unimpeded in all accomplishments and exceedingly bold; and, intent on seeing the fulfillment of his future purpose, he took up residence in that very cremation ground.
He guarded that skeleton of his.

Then one night at midnight, while he was awake with that same sense of wonder, Īśāna suddenly smelled the scent of divine incense and heard the sound of various musical instruments, such as the rattling of a *ḍamaru* drum.
As soon as he heard that sound, while he was opening the door to the darkness, he beheld a circle of yoginīs, radiant with a halo of light, assembled upon that ground in the cemetery.
It was seen.
Then, just as those yoginīs were about to strip away his skeleton, the Guru, sword in hand, arrived at that cremation ground while [the disciple] was still terrified.
Having arrived, he remained concealed by a tree and beheld that skeleton—its every limb being worshipped by the host of yoginīs—lying there in the mandala for that very reason.

When those *yoginīs*, who were deities afflicted by the intoxication of desire and longing for union with a supreme husband, could not find any other suitor, they then beheld that very skeleton. Then, in an instant, each of them placed one of their own limbs upon it; and having summoned from somewhere the splendor of a man (*puruṣalakṣmī*), they restored it to its full form.

Furthermore, the *yoginīs* used their yogic power to draw from somewhere that "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*)—which was wandering about because it had not yet entered a physical body—and established it within that wise Kaṅka.
They were there.

Then, like one awakened from sleep, that Sandhimati, having been anointed with divine unguents by them and assuming the leadership of the circle (*cakranāyakatva*), came to possess the attainment of enjoying them as he desired and so forth.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, that Lord (*īśāna*) [perceived] the division of his limbs and other parts bestowed by those yoginīs, which was being led away once again.
Being afraid and apprehensive, yet remaining steadfast for the sake of protection, he continued to roar at that very spot; and just as he arrived there, that host of yoginīs quickly vanished.
And as those yoginīs disappeared, he also heard this voice from them: "O Īśāna, let there be no fear for you."
Since there is no deficiency in the components of our ritual through this act, and indeed, alas, not even any deception,
but rather he is being joined with a divine body by our grace, this king shall be named Sandhimān; furthermore, he will become renowned on earth by the name Āryarāja due to his noble character.
Then Sandhimati, wearing celestial garments and celestial ornaments, garlanded and having regained his former memory, bowed down and paid homage to his own teacher.

Thereupon, the king, together with that teacher, engaged in a discourse on the worthlessness and insubstantiality of cyclic existence; and with the teacher’s consent, he—with great difficulty and free from desire—agreed to protect the kingdom. Thus it was described.
He who was the primary cause for the creation and other functions of this region—known as Īśeśvara—which possesses an inexpressible benefit to his Guru;
although Śiva, named Mahādeva, was previously established here, even now that place continues to be renowned by the name of that very Īśāna.
At present, the name of this region is celebrated throughout the entire world as Guptagaṅgā.
In that regard, because the Gaṅgā was protected (*guptā*)—that is to say, concealed (*gopitā*)—by Mahādeva, this name "Guptagaṅgā" is meaningful.
Having ascended the mountain named Mahādeva situated near that region, Mahādeva concealed the Gaṅgā.

Consequently, all the inhabitants of Kaśmīra consider the Gaṅgā located right there at Guptagaṅgā to be the [true] Gaṅgā itself, every year on the full moon of Vaiśākha during the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*).
People, including both children and the elderly, come there to bathe;
even now they call this place by the name Īśabhrāra.
In that regard, *bhrār* is the deity of *īśa*, which is *īśāna*; for in the Kashmiri language, the two words *bhroḥ* and *bhrār* are seen to exist in the sense of "deity" and "goddess" respectively.
In that case as well, one says *bhror devaḥ* (O God, brother! and *bhrār devī* (O Goddess, sister!).
Furthermore, since the word *devatā* is used in the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*) to denote the feminine gender, it is designated as feminine even in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*) by the form *bhrār*.
However, due to the corruption (*apabhraṃśa*) of this word *iś-bhrār*, village-dwellers call it *iśavara*.
Furthermore, there is this region where the Puragaṇa settlement is located; those who speak of that Puragaṇa call it by the name Phākpargaṇa.
This Puragaṇa is situated at a distance of three *krośas* from the city of Kaśmīra.
Here, travel to and fro occurs both by waterway via boats and by landway via horses and other such means.
This region, known as Niśātavāga, lies at a distance of three-quarters of a krośa from Pavana.
Here, there is one reservoir within, produced by coolness and shaped like a square;
furthermore, another such reservoir exists in the area adjacent to that inner reservoir.
Between both of these reservoirs, a small wall constructed of bricks, stones, and other materials remains visible even today;
however, ritual activities such as bathing are restricted solely to the outer reservoir,
while in the inner one, everyone performs only acts of worship and the like.

On the upper part of this reservoir, a temple built by an ancient king is still visible today, entirely undecayed and recognizable by its very form. The local elders and others there say that this shrine was constructed by King Sandhimati for the sake of his own preceptor; thus, from the records of the temple collection and other sources, Sandhimati himself is known to be the builder of this site.
Beyond this region there is yet another mountain;
for this very reason, this place appears to be at the foot of the mountain. At a certain distance from this mountain, there is also a sacred ford (tīrtha) named Gopītīrtha.
The villagers call his name *gupatrath* due to phonetic corruption.
Having gone a few paces from Īśāna-tīrtha, there is also a cave in the lower part [of the site].
Near that cave, there is also the house of Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇas known as the Sāhibs.
Those Brahmins never consume meat or similar foods.
Here, there is a temple currently being constructed by the modern king, which is already half-finished.
This pair of water reservoirs is now surrounded on all four sides by a wall.
14. *Loloraṃ* or *Lolaraṃ*:
Verse 86. Beginning from the eighty-fourth verse, in the description of the life of King Lava, it says "loloraṃ" or "lolaraṃ.
Therein is the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of *lolora*.
*Lolāḥ* means those with restless minds; *rānti* means they give, thus they are *rāḥ*, meaning givers.
*Na rāḥ* are *arāḥ*, meaning non-givers. *Loloraḥ* refers to that place where people who are both *lolāḥ* (restless) and *arāḥ* (non-givers) reside.

Alternatively, according to the *Ekākṣarakośa*, "the letter *la* is known by the ancient masters in the scriptures to signify 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) and 'fear' (*bhaya*). Thus, *la* here denotes both remainder and fear; in this regard, because this region stands as a remainder—that is, situated at the periphery—of this mandala, and because it is filled with fear due to paths such as extremely remote wildernesses and dense forests.
However, that which provides pleasure merely by the beauty of its location and so forth is also called *lolaras*.

Now, the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the second [type], named *lolarasa*: that which is restless (*cañcala*) due to various kinds of trees, creepers, shrubs, water, land, and other such features is *lola*.
That which gives the pleasure of delight by virtue of its extreme loveliness is *ra*;
that which is both restless (*lola*) and *ra* is *lolara*.
Since an exceedingly wonderful city was built in this region by the king named Lava, the understanding of the meaning here as "Lolara" or "Lavapura" is also entirely appropriate.
And likewise, in the eighty-fifth verse of the first book of the *Rājatarangiṇī* by Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa,
it is stated that he constructed the city of Lolara after completing ten million stone dwellings, minus one hundred and sixty thousand.

Based on the corruption of the word *Lavapura*, this name *Lolara* is inferred. Some [scholars] are translators of the *Rājatarangiṇī* composed in the Persian language. That king named Lava was always exceedingly fond of song.

Therefore, during the reign of that king, the people living in the city named Lolarā which he had founded, having perceived in every way King Tṛpta’s fondness for singing, made it their sole resolve to train in vocal performance; consequently, they all became experts in the science of song.
For this very reason, when it came to the singing of songs in the Kashmiri language, they began by uttering the name of that very king as "Lavalava" at the very start of the performance.

Over a long period of time, through the process of phonetic corruption (*apabhraṃśa*), the word for the king's name, "Lavalava," became clearly established as "Lolo. By that very word "Lolo," the region itself attained its renown.
Consequently, in their own manuscripts, they record that the name of this place is "Lolav," and so forth.

Even in modern times, it is well known to all that this word *luḥluḥ* in the Kashmiri language is used within songs both for the purpose of filling out a line and for addressing a beloved subject of description;
there is even a village of such a name in this group of villages (*puragaṇa*).
Because all people nowadays call it by the name "Lulu," for this reason as well, this entire cluster of villages has come to be designated by the term *lolava* according to its very name;
thus some villagers and city-dwellers maintain their own view.
Just as an entire group of villages (*puragaṇa*) comes to be designated by the name of a single village situated in its center, so too is it understood in other locations.
For instance, the group of villages known as Nāgām becomes denoted by the term "Nāgām" solely through the single village situated in its center called Kasava-nāgām.
However, the villagers themselves now proclaim the very name of this region, Lolār, as the "Lolav-pargaṇa."
Furthermore, the entire community of Puragaṇa bears the name of this village known as Lulur;
they call its name Lālpor.
In the midst of the route for coming and going through this region of Lolar, there is also a mountain.
Mounting upon which the coming and going of people occurs at all times,
this Puragaṇa lies between the two Puragaṇas known as Kramarājyasthapura and Khuyahoma;
for by way of these two aforementioned Puragaṇas, those desiring to travel obtain the path.

Since this region is situated on the frontier of the Krama kingdom, it is entirely appropriate that its etymology includes a description of its location and other such details as being "remaining" (śeṣa). However, as for what Kalhaṇa has written in his own book— that King Lava constructed a city by building eighty-four lakhs of stone houses, which is to say, a "peak" (koṭi) minus sixteen lakhs— [this is not so].
Those houses, due to the passage of an exceedingly long time in the modern era, have perished and are no longer seen at all;
however, many heaps of stones are observed everywhere, and thus it is known that those stones must be the remains and the surviving marks of those very houses.
The first village of this group of villages called Lolavpura is renowned by the name Khumariyāl, and the village at its end is famous by the name Lālporā.

In the center of this village of Khumariyāl, there is a reservoir of extremely cool water. Furthermore, in its very vicinity lies the village of Caṇḍī, which possesses a reservoir that serves as the abode of the goddess Caṇḍī.
In the local dialect of that village of Caṇḍī, it is known by the name Caṇāgom.
Many other villages such as these have likewise become abodes for deities; may there be peace.
15. Ledarī.
Verse number 87. Ledarī is the name of the very king Lava;
here is its etymological derivation.

According to the statement in the *Śivaproktakākṣarakośa*, "La is known as fear (bhaya) in the remaining [meanings]," *la* means fear; thus, *le* means in fear—that is to say, at the moment of producing fear. A cave (*darī*) speaks [of this].
That which is seen to be deep, dense, and difficult to cross is a *ledarī*.
Alternatively, according to the *Ekākṣarakośa*: "The letter *da* is declared by the wise to mean wife (*kalatra*), as well as gift (*dāna*), cutting (*chedana*), and giver (*dātṛ*)."

"Bhayacchedanā" means that which gives (*rāti*) the cutting off (*chedana*) of fear (*bhaye*); in other words, it means that river which, when fear has arisen, bestows its cessation. Such is the river.
Some say that because it relies upon the *Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā* of this Ledarī River, it is even called by the name Lambodarī.
In this context, "Lambodara" refers to Gaṇeśa, whose belly (*udara*) is hanging (*lamba*); the river issuing from his mouth is designated by the term Lambodarī.

On the route of the pilgrimage to Cāmareśvara, in the region known as Gaṇeśabalā, there is a large, highly venerable stone image of Gaṇeśa situated in the middle of the river, which is a famous manifestation.
This river, appearing as if vomited up from the trunk of that very form which visibly assumes the state of an elephant, shines forth;
moreover, this river possesses a name, *Ledari*, which is both etymologically justified and consistent with the *Saṃhitā*.
For in this group of cities called Dakṣiṇapārśva, where this river flows, there exists a village named Lidara situated on its banks; therefore, it is designated by that name.
This river has attained renown;
for it is the Ledārī River that flows through the village of Lidar.
Furthermore, in the *Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā*, during the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Mārtāṇḍa, this very name is used to designate the river.

For instance, as long as the river Ledarī flows filled with water; as long as the two twin lotuses remain inhabited by the two Nāgas called Matsya and Mukta; and as long as the sun constantly shines in the sky through the power of Time (kāla-śakti)—so long does one who performs the *śrāddha* rite dwell eternally in heaven within the Solar Field (*sūrya-kṣetra*). Such places are indeed indicators of the name "Ledarī"; specifically, it refers to the area between the two regions on the right bank of this very river.
This river flows;
however, in modern times, the villagers call this Ledarī or Lidarāra river Lambodarī.
Therein, the river which is filled in its middle with large boulders and flows with extreme velocity is difficult to cross.
They call that [river] by the name *ār* in the Kashmiri language;
and as for this village named Lidar, which serves as the site of this river, its name is likewise *lidar* in the local dialect of that village.
This village is said to be situated on the bank of the Ledari River, in the midst of the district known as Dacchunporpargana on its southern side.
Even for this Lambodarī, according to the view of the villagers, the name Lidar alone prevails, because this river comes from the region called Gaṇeśabala.
In the Kashmiri language, that place is known by the name Gaṇiśabal;
therein, *gaṇiśa* means Gaṇeśa, and *bala* means "place."

This region called Gaṇeśabala is the first stage of the journey to Amareśvara. Having traversed a distance of three *krośas* from here, the second stage of the journey to Amareśvara is the region called Pahalgāmā, which one reaches.
This village called Lidar lies twelve *krośas* to the west of Anantanāga.
Here, the temple known as Mandira is a vast stone structure that is nearly in ruins;
it was built at that site in the ninetieth year of Vikramāditya by King Meghavāhana, as described in the third chapter [of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*], and so forth.
It has been placed here, having been obtained from the collection of temples.
16. Levāraḥ. Verse number 87. In the life story of the one named Levāra, [this is] the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of that Levāra.

Regarding the statement "laḥ śeṣe ca bhaye khyātaḥ" (the sound *la* is known to denote the remainder and fear), and likewise from the *Ekākṣarakośa*: "vaḥ sāntvane rase vāte" (the sound *va* denotes consolation, taste, and wind)—he who gives (*rāti*) from the beginning up to the end (*āsamantāt*) the *levighna* (removal of obstacles) in the form of *va* (consolation), which is the warding off [of those obstacles], is *Levāra*. He is Gaṇeśa, the remover of obstacles.
And so it is stated in the *Nīlamata-vaṛṇya*, in the section titled "The Praise of the Abodes of Mānadeva":
"Bhūrjasvāmī, Hiḍambeśa, Levāra, Śrīvināyaka,
Utaṅkeśa, Guhāvāsī, Bhīmeśa, and likewise Saumukha."
Bhadreśvara, Mahāsya, Mahāśana, Gaveṣaṇa,
Paulastya, Girivāsī, Jayeśvara, and Maheśvara.
Having beheld each one of these Gaṇeśas with a well-composed mind,
one attains the accomplishment of one's purpose and enjoys the fruit of merit.
In such passages,

it becomes clear that this Gaṇeśa, known as Levārā, is described among the forms of Gaṇeśa located in Kaśmīra. This image of Gaṇeśa is well-known in that very region on the left bank of the aforementioned Ledari River, which is currently called Khourporpargaṇa in the vernacular usage of the local people.

It exists; by the very name of this Gaṇeśa, this village, which takes its refuge in the form of Gaṇeśa, has become renowned and established by the name Levar itself [...]. And this village, within this Puragaṇa, is called by the villagers by the term Levar.
Near this village there is another well-known village called Sīr;

at a certain distance from that very place, this village was already known by the name Levāra due to its being the residence of the Gaṇapati named Levāra, and it subsequently came to be designated as an *agrahāra* under that aforementioned Lavarāja.
For this very reason, Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa also states in the first *taraṅga*:
"Having bestowed the agrahāra of Levāra upon the assembly of twice-born in Ledarī,
that mighty-armed king, whose glory and valor were beyond reproach, ascended to heaven."

Thus it has been stated. By this very method, that village named Levā which had existed previously was established by the king at the time of the grant of the agrahāra to the Brāhmaṇas under its former well-known name.
Even at the time of giving alms, it is understood by the king that the very name of this place, called Levār, is designated as being based upon the form of Gaṇeśa;
and the local inhabitants say:
"In this village there is a great tree, which the Kashmiris designate by the word *braṇ*."
By that [tree] as well, he becomes indicated; that very tree also becomes the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for this aforementioned Gaṇeśa.
For many trees described by this *braṇvṛkṣa* are seen everywhere in the land of Kaśmīra serving as the loci for the forms of deities. May there be peace! (*śam*)
17. *Kuruhāraḥ*, verse number 88. Regarding the description of King Kuśa in *Kuruhāra*:
its etymological derivation (*nirvacana*).

And what is declared to be the "Self" (ātman), and what is cited as the "region" (pradeśa)? According to the *Kośa* [the Abhidharmakośa], it is by various kinds of regions such as water and land that he is "wide" (*uru*), great; for this reason, he is a "necklace" (*hāra*) and thus "captivating" (*manohara*). Therefore, he is the "Kuru-necklace" (*kuruhāra*). Furthermore, because of his intoxication with various regions, he is like a pearl necklace (*muktāhāra*) by means of the river Ledarī at its end; he too is the "Kuru-necklace."

Alternatively, *kuruhāra* refers to that which is taken away at the very outset (*agra*) by the inhabitants of the country named Kuru because it is a gift village (*agrahāra*). Formerly, the residents of this region bore the name "Kuru";
since the abundance of crops and other resources of this village was taken away by them at the very beginning, it is therefore also called *kuruhāra*.
For this very reason, the scholar Kalhaṇa also wrote his name in its full form as "Kuruhārāgrahāra," based on the statement: "Immediately after that, he became the donor of the agrahāra Kuruhāra."
For all agrahāras are designated as such precisely because their produce, such as grain, is taken away before the king's share is collected.
In modern times, all the villagers of this Kuruhāra region call it by the name *Kular* in their own language, a name known to all Kashmiris.
This village, called either Kuruhāra or Kular, is situated on the southern side and is universally referred to by people by the name *Dacchunporpargaṇa*.

In the vicinity of this village of Kular, there is another very famous village which people nowadays call by the name "Salar"; they are seen referring to it by a name well-known throughout the entire group of cities.
Both of these villages, known by the names Kular and Salar, come within the range of vision of pilgrims on the way to the pilgrimage of Amareśvara.

Moreover, for both of these villages, which have become sacred sites (*tīrtha*), there is a duty of performing ritual bathing, worship, and so forth, even without resorting to the pilgrimage of Amareśvara itself.
Due to the influence of phonetic corruption over a long period of time, the name "Kular" arose for this very region of Kuruhāra.

Some, however, state that the name of this region called Kuruhāra is "Kāṭhu. According to their view, "Kāṭhu" is simply the name of "Kular" itself, arising from the defect of long-standing phonetic corruption.

In reality, however, the similarity between the word *kuruhāra* and the word *kāṭhus* is perceived through its pronunciation in a way that is not apparent when compared with the word *kular*. Therefore, *kular* alone is the correct form; the name *kuruhāra* arises merely from the corruption of that term. Furthermore, this village called *kāṭhus* is also located within this very *dacchunpor* *pargana*, on the route to the pilgrimage site of *Amareśvara*.
Furthermore, for pilgrims, there exists the duty of performing rites such as bathing at the two aforementioned villages;
therefore, this third village, situated in close proximity to the two villages named Salarkula and Rāka, is designated as Kuruhār solely through error.
18. In the eighteenth verse, numbered 90, regarding the description of the reign of Khagendra, there is an etymological explanation of "Khagi":
here, "khaga" refers to one who goes (*gacchati*) in the sky (*khe*).

*Khaga* means one who goes (*ga*) in the sky (*kha*). Alternatively, he who goes everywhere in the sky (*kha*) is *khāga*. Viṣṇu is called *khāgī*, meaning that he possesses (*in*) the bird named Garuḍa, which is the vehicle of Viṣṇu.
Since this region maintains the status of being the seat of Viṣṇu’s form,
it has consequently attained renown by the very name of that Viṣṇu as Khāgī;
furthermore, there is the place named Garuḍāśrama, situated near this region and marked with the name of Garuḍa.
Because it is always in the vicinity of Garuḍa and serves as the vehicle for Viṣṇu, this place has attained renown by that name; therefore, the name "Khāgī" for this region appears most appropriate.
In this village famous as Khāgī, there is a medium-sized reservoir known to all people as Nārāyaṇakuṇḍa, which serves as the abode of an image of Viṣṇu.

The Kashmiris, however, state that in modern times the name of that Nārāyaṇakuṇḍa is known in their own language as *Nārāṇ Nāg*. Furthermore, this region bears the name *Khāg* due to its proximity to the aforementioned Garuḍāśrama. Just as the name of that Garuḍāśrama has arisen as *Khāg* through the corruption of the word *Garuḍī*, so too the villagers have [corrupted] the name Gaṇiśrama into *Khāg* by means of that same defect.
People speak of this everywhere;
therefore, these two places have been described. This site, known as Bahurūpa, has become a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) within the *puragaṇa* and exists even now.
Furthermore, the name "Bīrūpargaṇa," which was proclaimed by the villagers of this very *bahurūpapuragaṇa*, has remained in use until the present day.

In this group of cities known as Bahurūpa, it is universally renowned that they possess supreme majesty precisely because of the presence of such sacred sites (tīrthas) as the Nārāyaṇakuṇḍa and others. Accordingly, the *Nīlamata* states: "O best of men, having bathed at Bahurūpa, a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu; and this fruit has been declared regarding Bahurūpa."
And so forth.
This lake named Nārāyaṇanāga is quadrangular in shape; its water possesses an exceedingly cool touch and is likewise sweet in taste.
The mouth of this lake is constructed with large stones on all four sides.
This region appears surrounded by mountains resembling small desert plateaus upon the ground;
it is inferred that this place as well—bearing the ancient name Khāgi and designated as Rājāgrahāra—was established [by the king].
19. *Khonamuṣa*, verse 90, number 19. Regarding the description of the Lord of Birds (*khagendra*), this is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of *khonamuṣa*.
According to the authority of the *Kośa*: "The word *kha* is declared to mean a sense faculty (*indriya*); *kha* is said to mean space (*ākāśa*);
likewise, *kha* is spoken of as a garment, and *kha* is proclaimed to mean the void (*śūnya*).
Thus, one who is "devoid of" (*ūna*) or "lacking" (*rahita*) "clothes" (*khaiḥ*)—that is, garments—is *digambara*, meaning Śiva.

He who steals—that is, robs—the auspicious moon situated in the cave of the mountain is called *khonamuṣa*. Alternatively, he who steals by means of his own cool and captivating splendor the full moon—which is "non-non" (*nona*), meaning not empty (*khena śūnyaḥ*) but rather full—is also called *khonamuṣa*.
This region named *Khonamuṣa* is at the foot of the mountain; for "space" (*kha*) is declared to be the sense organ, and "space" (*kha*) is cited as the sky.
The word *kha* is declared to mean heaven; *kha* is also celebrated as meaning a serpent.
Likewise, they say *kha* refers to a chasm, and *kha* is proclaimed to mean emptiness.
It is situated below.
On this very upper peak of the mountain, there is a large, secluded cave devoid of light.
On the walls of that cave, the carved images of deities are visible all around.
Among those forms, one preeminent and great form of Śiva in the shape of a *liṅga*, bearing the name Harṣeśvara—renowned throughout all the maṇḍalas—is seen seated upon the ground.
Within this cave, there is another smaller cave;
in that small cave, the form of Śiva known as Svacchanda, adorned with five faces, appears as if outside, since entry into that small cave is [restricted].
This too is altogether difficult to accomplish.

Formerly, at the time of the destruction of the Asura named Bhasmasura, Śiva, in order to deceive that ill-born Asura who had been described [by him], kept his own form hidden within this cave for some time.
Then, when that wicked asura had been destroyed and he was filled with a great weight of joy, at that very moment the deity assumed the name Harṣeśvara.
Thus, it is understood that the name of this region, Guhyāśivamoṣaṇa, is indeed meaningful.
In modern times, the villagers of this region called Khonamuṣā even refer to this particular form of Śiva, known as Khunamoh, by the name Harimur.
The story of this Harṣeśvara is told in detail in the *Harṣeśvaramāhātmya* compiled within the *Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā*.
Near this Khonamoṣa, there is Jayavana, which is well known by the name *Jivan* in the Kashmiri language;
that village, as well as another village called Mābur, are situated nearby.
This village known as Khunamuh is renowned within the district (puragaṇa) called Vihī;
this village and its district are located at a distance of five krośas from the city of Kaśmīra. Thus [ends the description].
20. The Land of Darad (Daraddeśaḥ), verse 93, number 20. In the description of King Surendra, near the land of Darad; therein is the etymological derivation (nirvacana) of the land of Darad.
There is also the sense that "Darada" refers to the country which is the dwelling place of the Darada tribes;
indeed, there are many tribes known as Daradas who dwell among the mountains and other regions on the outskirts of the city of Kaśmīra.
Many countries serving as their bases outside of Kaśmīra in the frontier territories have become renowned by the very name "Darada."
And in modern times, they call the region inhabited by those people of the Darada race by the name *Dāradisthāna* in the Kashmiri language;
furthermore, the name *Dārada* is well-known everywhere for the people residing in that country. Likewise, it is also stated in the *Nīlamata*:
The Dārvas, Abhisāras, Gāndhāras, Juhuṇḍaras, Śakas, Khaśas, Taṅgaṇas, Māṇḍavas, Madras, and those dwelling in the inner and outer mountains.
Having said this, those regions and districts that have been enumerated as dependencies are inferred to be of the Darada race alone.
All the bases for these and others are designated by the very term "Darada country.
Therefore, this region has always remained subject to the commands of the kings of Kaśmīra.
For this very reason, it is understood that the King of Kaśmīra has always been the one who exercises authority over the land of Darad.
21. Sauraka. Verse 93, number 21: During the reign of Surendra, there was a city named Sauraka.
Herein follows the etymological derivation of the word "Sauraka."

Based on the statements of the lexicon (*kośa*)—"He is *saḥ* (he) in the sense of restraint (*vāraṇa*) and indeed in the sense of anger (*kopa*)," "The syllable *oṃ* is likewise *brahmā*," and "Bliss (*ānanda*) is also called *au*," as well as "Who is declared to be the Self (*ātman*)? and "What is cited as the region (*pradeśa*)?"—[the term] *sauraka* is explained as follows: he who restrains (*vāraka*) from suffering is *sau*; he who bestows (*rāti*) that bliss (*ānanda*) which is *au* is *sora*;
and such a one who is the region (*pradeśa*) is *sauraka*.
