That is to say, a region that wards off suffering and bestows bliss; or else, one like Saura (the son of Sūra), namely Saturn (Śani), or one resembling Sopama—referring to a place that is difficult to behold due to its desolation, and which, by possessing wildernesses, thickets, and the like, is comparable to the earth and appears dark and soiled like Saturn; what such a region might be? Thus it is said.
This very city is such a *pattana*;
according to Amara, *pattana* means a port-city (*puṭabheda*).
The intended meaning is that the Lord of the Gods (Indra) carved this out upon the forehead of the previously described land of Darada.

It is understood from the very words of the scholar Kalhaṇa that the city named Sauraka was established separately by the king in the land of the Darads, which lies at a preeminent site within the Kaśmīra region; for it is said:
"Having established the city named Sauraka near the land of the Darads..."
The illustrious one established a monastery here named Narendra-bhava.
Furthermore,
by him— whose fame was unblemished within his own realm and who performed meritorious deeds—
a magnificent monastery named Sora was constructed with great effort.
Because of such statements, this king’s manifestation and other [miraculous deeds] occurred both in his own realm called Kaśmīra and elsewhere in the land of Darad.
Everyone speaks of the most famous name of this city called Sauraka in the language of Kaśmīra as *Hasaur*.
Furthermore, there exists a city named Hasaur in the land of Darad.
Even this country of Darad is well known by the names Dāradyan, Hundradeśa, or Dāradyan-hundramūlaka.

Furthermore, those countries such as Haṇu, Gilgit, Hauja, Karṇāha, and others, although situated apart from the Kaśmīra maṇḍala, are indeed reckoned as being within the kingdom of Kaśmīra; likewise, they always remain subject to the commands of the ruler of this maṇḍala.
Therefore, it is most appropriate that the construction of a city for that king should take place in the Darad country.
However, some who are experts in the *Pāriseka-anuvāda*— being ignorant of this city called Sauraka and, due to a confusion of intellect and their own baseless, fanciful imaginings—
have falsely conceived of a certain region named Sindhu-sura as being the referent of the word "Sauraka."
They write that a region called Sindhuṣura was created for the king, and so forth; however, all of their writing is utterly untrue,
because in the description of Surendra as recounted in the *Rājatarangiṇī*, no such creation of a territory is seen anywhere.
Therefore, even without knowing the specific purpose here, one understands that such is his [the opponent's] view.

22. The Monastery named Narendra-bhavana, Verse 93, Number 22: In the kingdom of Surendra, there was a monastery named Narendra-bhavana; here follows the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the term *Narendra-bhavana*.
*Narendra* means the lord (*indra*) of men (*narāṇām*), that is, of human beings;
*narendrabhavana* is the palace or residence of the lord of men, meaning the royal palace.
Just as kings have their own dwellings inlaid with gold, silver, jewels, and so forth, according to the purest craftsmanship.
Just as [buildings] are constructed by artisans, so too did the king, the lord of the gods, having built a city named Hasaura near the country of Darad,
construct there a monastery called Narendrabhavana— the meaning of which is a house for the use of Buddhist people, such as their dwellings;
for among Buddhists, the word *vihāra* refers to a dwelling.
According to the *Amara-kośa*, "gañjā" means a house for liquor;
a Buddhist temple of that kind was also constructed.
And there exists a place called Narendrabhavana in the vicinity of the city named Hasaura, situated in the middle of the Darad country.
And in modern times, according to the Kashmiri tradition, that royal palace (narendrabhavana) is known by the name Nagūr.
Since that region called Nagūr is located in the vicinity of Hasaur, it is for this very reason that the region designated by the term "royal palace" appears to be that very place.

In this same manner, he will later describe how the King had the construction of his own palace site carried out within the territory of the Darad country, specifically between the two regions named Hasaur and Nagūr, as a place set apart from his own domain.
23. The Sorasa Monastery, Verse 94, Number 23. During the reign of Surendra, there was a monastery named Sorasa.
Regarding that, first is the etymological derivation of the word "Sorasa."

According to the lexicon (kośa), "sa" means both anger and restraint. "So" refers to the restrainer (*vāraka*) of heat and so forth, as well as thirst and so forth. Furthermore, according to the lexicon, "ū" is said to mean Śaṅkara, and "ū" also means the protector (*rakṣaka*);
thus, "ū" means the protector, which is to say, life itself.

And likewise, according to the *Medinīkośa*, which states: "The word *rasa* [is used] for taste, fragrance, water, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and so forth; for poison, potency, the bitter and other tastes, fluidity, color, a specific constituent of the body, mercury, and flavor," [the name] *Saurasa* means "he whose *rasa* is water.
Here, the word *rasa* is taken in the sense of "water" according to the *Amara-kośa*, which states: "*rasa* means life, the world, and the forest."

Since the word *jala* (water) has the same meaning as the word *jīvana* (life), and since the words *rakṣaka* (protector) and *jīvana* (life) are synonymous, the qualification "protector" (*rakṣaka*) is indeed appropriate. Therefore, the meaning is: a region containing Buddhist monasteries known by names such as *Vihāra*, which bring water that wards off heat and other [calamities].
In modern times, the villagers call this region named Sora by the name *Suras Yār* in the Kashmiri language.

In this region, the river named Dugdhagaṅgā flows, its waters cool to the touch and sweet in taste; because Pārvatī also flows there, the name Sorasa is meaningful for this river that bears the name Dugdhagaṅgā. Among the Kashmiris, it is renowned by the name Dūdgaṅgā.
This region called Sora lies within the city-group named Nāgo;
there too, it is at the foot of a mountain.
Near this Sora, there are two villages known as Ḍāḍa Um Pūr and Mici Um Pūr.

24. The Agrahāra named Hastiśālā, verse 96, number 24: In the description of King Godhara, [there is] the Agrahāra named Hastiśālā. Therein is the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word "Hastiśālā."

An *hastiśālā* is a place where elephants (*gaja*) "shine" (*śālante*), meaning they are beautiful; it is the form of the verbal root *śāl* in the sense of praise. Alternatively, an *hastiśālā* is the hall (*śālā*) of elephants, that is to say, the house or dwelling place of elephants.
The meaning is that such a land-grant (*agrahāra*) was established by King Godhara and, having been established, given to the Brahmins.

Herein lies the intention: because the place suitable for the maintenance of those rut-maddened elephants, female elephants, and young calves that were in this king's household was restricted to this very region, therefore [it was given] to this region.
The name "Hastiśāla" has become attached [to this place]. Furthermore, in the district known as Devasarasa, there exists a village named Hastiśālā;
and in modern times, that district called Devasarasa is known by the name "Devasarpargaṇa" in the local dialect.
Likewise, this village known as Hastiśālā also has a name well-known to all, namely Hastyhel;
near this village of Hastyhel is a village called Kulagrāma,
which the people now call by the name Kulgom, maintaining its status as the primary village and the seat of this entire Devasarpagaṇa.
That village is nearby.
In this village named Hastiśālā, there is a very famous great reservoir called Ḍal;
it is unknown to all Kashmiris except for those in the Phākpuragaṇa, and on its banks are [places] such as Niśātbāg and Śālabāg.
Many highly renowned monasteries (ārāmas) are still seen even today;
they say that there is one particular area on the bank of that very same reservoir which is called by this [name] "Hastihelā.
However, although this area named Hastiśālā must certainly have been written as belonging to the reservoir called Ḍal, [it is not so].

On the bank, at a short distance from the region renowned as Ratabal— a preeminent locality on that very shore— and yet in close proximity to the place there called Āśiyabāg, there is indeed [this site]; nevertheless, because this elephant stable here is largely composed of water and displays a lack of suitable space and so forth, it is impossible for it to serve the purpose of an elephant stable.

Furthermore, because that [other] region, which consists mostly of water, is unfit to be bestowed upon Brahmins, it is precisely this [present] agrahāra named Hastiśālā— situated within the district of Devasarapura and established by King Godhara— that shines forth;
it is not some other region named Hastiśālā, which is watery and thus unfit for the designation of an agrahāra.

Furthermore, even according to the view following the Pāriseka-anuvāda, it is recorded that the construction of the Godhāra royal grant was made for Hastiśāla alone, which originated from Devasaras, and not for this other [place] belonging to the Phākpur group; may there be prosperity.
25. *Suvarṇamaṇikulyā*, verse 97, number 25. Regarding the description of the kingdom as golden, there is the *suvarṇamaṇikulyā*.
In that context, this is the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the term *suvarṇamaṇikulyā*.
That which possesses a beautiful color is *suvarṇa*; it is *kāñcana*, *svarṇa*, *suvarṇa*, and *kanaka*—this refers to the jewel-gem (*maṇiratna*).
According to Amara: "The words *ratna* and *maṇi* both apply to two kinds of things born from stone, and also to pearls and the like.
A *kulyā* is a small river or an artificial stream of gold and gems.
According to Amara, "kulyā" means a small, natural stream;

by this, it is meant that the river known as Suvarṇamaṇikulyā was brought into existence by the king named Suvarṇa. In this context, it refers to the river whose banks, bed, and ground were beautified and constructed with gold and jewels, and which was thus set in motion by him.

Alternatively, upon close examination, it is understood that the name of this river is indeed significant, for that river possesses water as pure in color as gold and as stainless and enchanting as a gem. Here, his son named Suvarṇa (Gold) was born; he became a "Golden River" for those in need, being the one who set flowing the stream of golden gems from Karāla.
Thus says Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa.
In his description of King Suvarṇa’s kingdom, having referred to the Suvarṇamaṇikulyā,
he writes in such a way that the very understanding arises in the mind that this canal must necessarily flow through the region named Karāla.

However, although this river still flows even today through that group of cities, despite searching with great effort and exertion throughout that entire group of cities, no such place or village named Karāla is found anywhere.
Therefore, the understanding that the Suvarṇamaṇikulyā flows through a place named Karāla appears to be entirely meaningless, arising from a delusion.
However, from the perspective of the true meaning, the intention of the poet Kalhaṇa may be inferred as follows:
according to the Amarakośa, *karāla* means "uneven" (*dantura*) or "swift" (*tura*).
Thus, any region whatsoever that is exceedingly high is what is designated by the word *karāla*.
Thus, the understanding that the river was indeed caused to flow by the king at the high place called Karāla appears most appropriate;

for since this river flows from all the lands of Kaśmīra onto the primordial ground which is exceedingly higher than them, the poet’s description of the river flowing upon the high ground synonymous with Karāla is in every way consistent.

In this land of Kaśmīra, which in former times existed in the form of a lake when no land whatsoever had yet come into being, it was through the compassion of the triad of deities propitiated by the sage Kaśyapa that land first appeared; and because it was from that very land [that the earth emerged], the name "Avani" (the Earth) became attached to it in its literal sense even to this day.
Since she exists at the beginning, she is "Ādyā"; and she is that very "Avanī," meaning the earth (*bhūmi*).
According to Amara, *kṣmā*, *avanī*, *medinī*, and *mahī* are synonyms;
thus, *avanī*, *medinī*, and *mahī* are all [names for the earth].
Therefore, the original name of this group of villages was *Ādyāvanī*, meaning "the first land.
In modern times, the name by which this group of villages, *Ādyāvanī-puragaṇa*, is known among both urbanites and rural folk—namely, *Āḍavinpargaṇa*—is rooted in the corruption of that original term.
Furthermore, there is a river called the Suvarṇamaṇikulyā, which is celebrated in the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūpa; this river is universally renowned by the name *Sunamaṇ Kul* or *Sunamaṇ Nor*.
In that regard, in the first case, the meaning is that there is a river named Sunaman;
in the second, however, the meaning is that there is a water-channel named Sunaman.
Regarding these two, Amara states: "The word *praṇālī* refers to a channel for water."
However, because this river called Suvarṇamaṇikulyā flows through only a single village of this group of towns, there is no fixed boundary for it.

In many villages of this group of towns, the production of crops and other goods is possible solely through the waters of the river named Sunamaṇ, which has been described [in the records]. Even in the accounts of irrigation works, it is stated that the king ensured the flow of the Sunamaṇ river into this very Ādyāvanipu group of towns so that the abundance of the fruits of the crops in those various locations might always come from it.
They describe [the matter] as being done with a specific intention (*abhiprāyeṇa*), and so forth.

For this reason as well, the flowing of the river in the region called Karālā appears to be entirely meaningless; for even by them, at the time of their respective descriptions, no such place named Karālā was ever found.

Therefore, in whatever way it may be, it is the very surface of the earth that is intended here by the word *karāla*; such is the intention of the poet Kalhaṇa, who is skilled in discerning the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). May there be peace.
26. Jālora Monastery and Agrahāra, Verse 98, Number 26. In the description of the progenitor of Suvarṇaja, [the text mentions] the monastery named Jālora and the agrahāra;
herein is the etymological derivation of the word "Jālora."

Because he was a protector (*rakṣaka*) from foul odors and the like by means of nets (*jāla*) and networks of flowers (*puṣpajāla*), he was called Jāla; for this very reason, he was a giver of pleasure (*rasa-sukha-dāyaka*), thus [being] Sujālora. According to the lexicon (*kośa*): "The letter *ū* indeed signifies a protector. Alternatively, a "net" (*jāla*) is a collection of waters (*jalānām*); by that net, he was a protector (*ū-rakṣaka*) and a bestower of pleasure (*rasa-sukhaprada*).
In this very place called Jālorā, a Buddhist monastery named Vihāra was built by that king, and it has become renowned as the Jālorā Agrahāra.
In modern times, the inhabitants of this village of Jālor call it by the well-known name "Jālu.
This village of Jālor is situated within the Śamālāpura gaṇa;
and the name of that gaṇa called Śamālā has been established by them as "Hamalpargaṇa" due to the influence of phonetic corruption (apabhraṃśa).

This village of Jālur is sometimes seen being filled by the waters of the great Padma lake, whether from its surging waves or from the [subterranean] Nāga; therefore, because of the presence of a mass of water (*jala-samūha*), the etymological derivation of this region as "Jāla" (a collection of waters) is most appropriate.
In the vicinity of this village of Jālur, there exist many neighboring villages such as Uccha, Kuṇḍala, Markuṇḍala, and others—may all be well.
27. *Śamāṅgāsaḥ*.
Verse number 100, number 27. Regarding the description of Śacīnara, the son of Janaka, there is the term *śamāṅgāsaḥ*;
here follows the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the word *śamāṅgāsaḥ*.

*Śama* is the cessation of the mind from various kinds of conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpa*), mental fluctuations (*vikalpa*), and so forth, because the verbal root *śamu*, meaning "to pacify," denotes the sense of coming to rest.

Likewise, those sages (*munayaḥ*) whose limbs (*aṅgāni*) possess such tranquility are called "tranquil" (*śāntāḥ*); they are designated by the term *śamāṅga*. They dwell there, and thus that place is called *śamāṅgāsaḥ*, which means, in effect, the dwelling place of the tranquil sages.

This region is adorned solely by wild trees such as the *sarala* and others; for this very reason, it is largely forested, characterized by austerity (*tapas*), and capable of supporting ascetic practice.
The entire group of villages (*puragaṇa*) in which this region lies, known by the name Kuṭahāra, also appears almost always entirely surrounded by forest areas.

Therefore, the name of this group of villages—meaning "a necklace (*hāra*) made of peaks (*kuṭa*)," i.e., mountain summits—is indeed meaningful. In modern times, its name has become universally renowned as *Kuṭahāraparganā*.

They say that even for this region of Śamāṅgāsa, its now well-known name "Śāṅgāsa"— which has arisen from the corruption of speech— is universally recognized. This village called Śāṅgāsa is situated on the very surface of the earth at the foot of a mountain of modest height.

The form and beauty of this region are exactly like those of the forests situated elsewhere in this Kaśmīra; for that very reason, its meaningful name is "The Abode of Sages" (*munijanani-vāsasthāna*).
In this region, all the inhabitants of the city named Śobhana always [reside] for the sake of hunting and other pursuits.
It should be understood that this region is most famous because many are seen coming and going and engaging in hunting here.
In the vicinity of this place called Śāṅga, there are many well-known villages such as Navgām, Urtus, Cerapor, and others.

Furthermore, although this village named Śamāṅgā was already recognized by sages as a fit place for the practice of austerities and thus designated as their own residence, it was [further] designated by King Janaka as his principal agrahāra.
He was entrusted with them; that is to say, this entire community of Puras was handed over to those ascetics residing in that region,
as they were dear to the ascetics and serve as a place for their ascetic practices even today in villages such as Uturus and others.
These ascetics are the disciples of former ascetics marked by the *nandī* [symbol]; their lineage continues even today through the succession of disciples and grand-disciples. Thus, peace.
28. Aśanāraḥ.
Verse 100. Regarding the description of this very Śacīnara, [there is] Aśanāraḥ.
Therein is its etymological derivation (nirukti).
That which is eaten or consumed is "aśana," meaning food; this is the form of the root *aś* (to eat) with the suffix *lyuṭ*.
The desire for food is "aśanāyā," meaning hunger.
Amara states: "Aśanāyā, bubhukṣā, and kṣudh are synonyms for hunger."
And likewise, *aśanā* is simply hunger (*aśanāyā*). He who gives (*rāti*) that hunger from all sides (*ā*) is *aśanāraḥ*.

In this region, there is water which flows; because of its extreme power of digestion, it possesses the quality of digesting the four kinds of food and so forth once consumed—a fact which everyone residing there acknowledges.
For this very reason, the fact that it produces hunger appears as the very meaning of the suffix -mat in the designation "aśanārī" which is about to be mentioned.
This region called Aśanārī is situated within the group of cities known as Vyūha;
and the name of that group of cities known as Vyūha is proclaimed by the villagers as "Vihīpargaṇa."
Even for this place called Śār, those who speak of it from all sides are seen to be in great poverty;
furthermore, there is a mine of iron in this village of Śār.
There is even a mountain characterized by those very same stones from which iron is produced through smelting and other processes.
Therefore, whatever water produced from the iron mine belongs to this village is necessarily the best for cooking among all places;
thus, the name of the village, Aśanāra, exists in accordance with its literal meaning.
Near this village of Śārga is a famous village called Maṇḍikhapāl, and another village, Luḍhav, is also situated nearby.
29. Śuṣkaletra:
Verse 102, number 29, regarding the description of King Aśoka;
therein is the etymological explanation of Śuṣkaletra.
The wind is called *śuṣkala* because it takes (*lāti*) or seizes (*ādatte*) dry things such as grass and leaves that have become parched;
this is a form of the verbal root *lā*, meaning "to take.
Furthermore, according to the lexicon, the vowel *ī* is said to signify *lakṣmī*.
*Īr* means *lakṣmī* (fortune); *īḥ* means wealth (*sampatti*). *Śuṣkala* refers to the wealth of wind (*vāyu-sampat*), meaning a great mass of wind.
He protects (*trāyate*) that wealth of wind in *śuṣkala*; thus he is *śuṣkaletraḥ*. The verbal root *traiṅ* is used here in the sense of "to protect."
Since this region is situated in a desert wasteland, it is therefore filled with great winds; such is the meaning.
This very region was covered by King Aśoka with Buddhist shrines (devāyatana) designated as *stūpas*.
In modern times, the name of this region called Śuṣkaletra has become known among the villagers as Hukhalitar.
This village named Hukhalitar is situated in the district (puragaṇa) called Daiñcho;
this district lies at a distance of exactly four *krośas* from the city of Kaśmīra.
In the vicinity of this village of Hukhalitar, there are other villages such as Śīlypūr and others.
In this entire group of cities, located everywhere in the desert region, the wind is more powerful and intense than in other lands;
for this very reason, it is appropriately named Śuṣkaletra, a name that signifies the actual presence of an abundance of wind. Thus [ends the explanation].
30. Vitastātraḥ, verse number 102, folio 30. During the reign of Aśoka was Vitastātra. Therein is the etymological explanation of Vitastātra.
According to the statement of Amarasiṃha, "the thumb [length] should be [one unit], and with the little finger [added], it is a *vitasti* of twelve *aṅgulas*.
Thus, for every person, twelve *aṅgulas* measured by their own [hand] are designated by the word *vitasti*.
A river measured by that *vitasti* standard is what is denoted by the term *Vitastā*.

And likewise, in the *Nīlamata*, in the description of the manifestation of Satī Devī in the form of the Vitastā, Bṛhadaśva says: "Having understood this truth, she, purified by supreme forbearance, spoke to her husband, her face resembling the lovely moon: 'O Teacher of the World, I shall take the form of a river in the subterranean realm (rasātala).
O Kuru, deliver a blow with your hand near the Blue House (nīlaveśma), where there was previously the ploughshare-shaped opening made by the Lord for cleaving the mountain.'"

"By that blow of the trident, having emerged from the subterranean realm (rasātala), I shall go by way of the trident-path as far as the great river Sindhu. When Śarva had spoken thus, the auspicious Satī acted accordingly;
Śaṅkara himself gave her the name Vitastā.
Hara dug a pit one *vitasti* in depth with his trident, through which that best of rivers emerged from the subterranean realm (*rasātala*). Therefore, the name "Vitastā" was given to her.
O Sage, news of this great goddess having arisen spread throughout all lands; out of affection for the sage, she then caused herself to flow across the country once more.

In various regions, people heard with great curiosity the account that the virtuous goddess, having become a river, emerged from Kaśmīra; thus it is established that the name *Vitastā* for this river is indeed etymologically significant. However, it should be understood here that these twelve fingers' breadth [of the image] correspond to twenty-five years of age for a man measured by the *vitasti*.

He who protects this very Vitastā as it has been described—both by holding her aloft as a mine and by supporting her—and who nourishes her even with the filling of water in the form of a stream, is the *vitastātra*.
Here too, the root is the same as before: *trai* (to protect).

Although in this region known as Vitastātra, when it had become a riverbed, only a pit measuring a *vitasti* was ever seen after only a few years had passed, even so, a great reservoir constructed by the ruler of Kashmir named Śrī Raṇavīrasiṃha, who resides in heaven, is now visible.
However, prior to the time of this king’s new constructions and restorations, the trench was only twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) deep;

therefore, those statements in the *Nīlamata Purāṇa* and the *Vitastāmāhātmya* that describe the dimensions of the river appear consistent and accurate. Nowadays, both the urbanites and the villagers call this region named Vitastātra by the name Vithavatur.
In this regard, the etymological connection is also consistent with the Kashmiri language, which states that *vith* means "a source of the Vitastā" (*vith-vitastāyāḥ vatur ākaraḥ*).
This village named Vithavatur is situated at the junction of two groups of districts (*puragaṇa*), namely those known as Śāhūbād and Devasaras.

There, this group of districts belonging to Śāhūbād is renowned by the name Śrī Raṇavīrasiṃhapura, while this group of districts belonging to Devasaras is known by the name Divasarpa; these two names are current today.
Everyone says this at the proper time;
some who record the *pāriṣeka-anuvāda* write the name of this region called Vitastātra as "Vatarahel" in their own books.
That village, Vatarahel, is situated within the *puragaṇa* known as Daiñcho.
Therefore, this village called Śuṣkaletra— or rather, the village named Hukhalitarā, as previously described—
is its location; or else, because it is mentioned together with the village of Vithavatu, it refers to one [monastery] named Aśoka in both of these regions.

Because the King was the creator of this transformation, people in the district of Daiñchopura consider even this region of Vitastātra to be situated there due to the aforementioned delusion, and thus they establish their own position by calling Vitastātra "Vatarahel.
However, since the very name of the Vitastā does not exist at all within that entire district of Daiñchopura, how indeed can we explain the name of Vitastātra as being "Vatarahel"?
Therefore, let it suffice to say that their writing appears to be nothing more than a fabrication of their own imagination.

Furthermore, certain other followers of that same school are observed to mistakenly believe this region called Vitastātra to be Vithanār; they maintain that it is distinct from the Vatarahela region and assert that "Vithanār" is indeed the name of this Vitastātra.
In this context, *vith* means a channel for the Vitastā;
there exists a region called Vithanārā, situated on the bank of the Vitastā river at a distance of one *krośa* from the city of Kaśmīra.
Regarding this, the elders say that in former times, when the waters were swollen each year by the rains of the month of Jyeṣṭha...
At that time, as this river Vitastā was swelling and was on the verge of submerging the entire region, the kings who were then ruling Kashmir commanded artisans to construct a canal-like channel.
By those very artisans, a channel in the form of a small irrigation trench was constructed, which averted the danger of flooding caused by the water rising from the lamp.
The name *Vithanāra* is attached to that very canal (*kulyā*) according to the manner described [in the text]. Here,
by Kalhaṇa’s mention of "the circles of stupas spread out on the dry banks of the Vitastā" and so forth, there exists this region called *Vataraheḷa*, as well as this region named *Vithanāra*.
Both of these appear equally unworthy of being covered by a Buddhist shrine (stūpa), as designated by that term:
for the first, named Vatarahel, because it lacks the support of the Vitastā River, it is utterly unfit for such a ritual function;
and for the second, named Vithanār, because it consists of an irrigation canal (kulyā) or watercourse, it is fit to serve as the foundation for a stūpa.

Therefore, it is established that this village of Vithavatu itself is what is denoted by the term Vitastātra, because only that [village] possesses the possibility of being the site for a stūpa, and no other does; may there be peace.
31. Dharmāraṇya Monastery (Vihāra), Verse 103, No. 31. During the reign of this aforementioned King Aśoka, a caitya was constructed at Vitastātra-pura within the Dharmāraṇya Monastery.
First, here is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the term "Dharmāraṇya Monastery."
Dharma is the collection of ritual acts approved by compassionate and truly wise persons who are free from passion and hatred, which brings about heaven, liberation, and so forth.
"Dharmāraṇya" is the forest of Dharma;
for Amarasimha states: "Aṭavī, araṇya, vipina, gahana, kānana, and vana are synonyms for forest."
Just as in a forest there is the presence of all wild animals, birds, trees, shrubs, grasses, and so forth,

even so, where there is the existence of all those things that constitute the limbs of Dharma— such as ritual purity, bathing, and the like— it is therefore called a *dharmāraṇya*, meaning a forest of Dharma. Furthermore, according to Amara, a dwelling used by Buddhists is called a *vihāra* for the Buddhists.
The meaning is "in the midst" or "within" such a Dharmāraṇya monastery.
And thus, in Vitastātrapura—as previously described, in this very region called Vitastātra—that King Aśoka established the monastery named Dharmāraṇya; [this refers to] the Dharmāraṇya monastery.

Likewise, when the establishment of Vitastātrapura— which served as its foundation— had been accomplished, [it was said] "the caitya which was built," meaning the shrine (devatāyatana) constructed by King Aśoka himself.
According to Amara, *caitya* and *āyatana* are synonyms, while *vājiśālā* and *mandura* refer to a stable.
And such indeed was this caitya that the eyes of the people who beheld its ultimate height became powerless;
even with effort they could not reach it. Thus, here too, the account of Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa concerns a structure within the Dharmāraṇya monastery at Tripureśvara on the Vitastā, regarding which he says:
"The caitya he built was such that the eye was incapable of reaching its limit of elevation."

Having constructed a Buddhist monastery named Dharmāraṇyavihāra in the city of Vitastātra, that king built a similarly lofty stūpa within that very monastery, such that the eyes of people desiring to behold its height were unable to reach its summit.
The meaning is that, due to its extreme height, that stūpa lay far beyond the range of vision.
However, in modern times, not even the name of this very ancient construction is found anywhere;
for here in Vitastātra-pura, there is not even the slightest sign or trace of the former structure to be seen.
It is only due to the delusions of certain individuals that the name of this region has been written as "Vatarahel" or "Vithanār" in their own books.
In both of those regions, even with minute scrutiny, neither the name of a monastery (*vihāra*), a shrine (*caitya*), nor anything else is seen or heard.
Therefore, the name "Gift of the Four Monasteries" for this region of Vitastā is not inconsistent;

on the contrary, it is perfectly appropriate in its literal sense, because there is an absence here of any signs such as monasteries or shrines known by the name Dharmāraṇya-vihāra, due to the power of the vast period of time that has elapsed.
That which is to be awakened to.
32. Śrīnagarī, verse 104, number 32: During the reign of this very Aśoka, [he established] Śrīnagarī.
First, here is the etymological derivation of the word "Śrīnagarī."
Those mountains and hills which do not go anywhere bestow great splendor upon that city;
for "nagara" means a small city, just as "ghaṭa" refers to a small jar or pot—as stated in the *Amarakośa*:
"pūḥ, strī, purī, nagarī, or pattana, puṭabhedana."
The word *nagarī* also denotes a city; thus, "Śrīnagarī" means that city which is both glorious (*śrīmatī*) and a city (*nagarī*).

The meaning is that King Aśoka constructed such a city named Śrīnagarī. Furthermore, [the buildings] were radiant with a fully developed luster due to their splendor, beauty, and abundance of all necessary resources, and they were works executed by highly skilled artisans.
The meaning is that the city was constructed as one filled with and resplendent with those very houses— ninety-six lakhs in number— which were characterized by their great merit.
And thus, Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa has written here:
That illustrious king made the city Śrīnagarī exceedingly magnificent with ninety-six lakhs of houses, resplendent with wealth.
And so forth.
For this very reason, it is known through poetic expression that this king was the creator of the construction of more than ten thousand cities.
This has been proclaimed by both rural and urban dwellers in the present day concerning the city renowned as Śrīnagarī.
Likewise, the name "Śrīnagara," which is well-known throughout all other regions, exists in every respect;
however, no specific, fixed location for this city called Śrīnagara can be found.
Therefore, it is understood that there is no such city distinct from this region known as Kaśmīra.
By the very name of this city created by Aśoka, this entire region became renowned and established.

For this very reason, the name "Śrīnagara" has become clearly manifest, proclaimed by the inhabitants dwelling in all directions throughout the land of Kaśmīra. Except for the Kaśmīrians themselves, everyone else refers to this region by this very name, Śrīnagara; and those who are translators of the Pārisika [Persian] and their followers likewise use it in their own books.

They write that the two sides— the right side and the left side— upon which this country named Śrīnagara is situated, are currently those very districts known as the *puragaṇas* of Dacchunpor and Khourpor; such is what they mean.
These two groups of fortresses that exist are indeed named Śrīnagarī;
or rather, their intention is that due to the great antiquity of [the city], these two groups of fortresses serve as the very marks of that country called Śrīnagarī.
However, the scholar Kalhaṇa does not write even a single word in his own book to the effect that the right and left sides alone are designated by the name Śrīnagarī, and so forth.
Therefore, it is clear that the view of those who advocate for "sprinkling" (pāriṣeka) is merely a fabrication of their own imagination; all is well.
33. Aśmamayaḥ Prākāraḥ, verse number 105, serial number 33: During the reign of this [king] Aśoka, there was a stone wall (*aśmamaya-prākāra*).
This is its etymological explanation.

That in which stones abound, or that whose material is stone, is "stone-made" (*aśmamaya*). Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of "abounding in this" or "having this as its material. A stone-made wall (*prākāra*) means a rampart (*sāla*).
"A rampart, a fence, a wall"—thus says Amara. Such a rampart was constructed by that King Aśoka.
Here, in that very region of Vijayeśvara—which was previously described as being twelve *nambara*s in extent and named Vijayeśvara—by former kings...
A wall made of plaster was constructed;
having demolished that plaster wall, the king caused a new wall made of stone to be built.
And so says the scholar Kalhaṇa:
Having had the dilapidated plaster coating of Śrī Vijayeśa removed,
he caused a stone wall to be constructed by Niṣkalmaṣa.
Thus,
because this rampart has been destroyed in modern times, even its name cannot be found;
let alone any report concerning its marks or features.
Therefore, it should be understood that the name and other details of this place as they exist at the present time have not been recorded by people.
However, because there was once a stone wall here in some ancient period, it has been included in this collection of regional sites;
just as, in modern times, the temple of Śiva built by King Śrī Raṇavīrasiṃha is counted among the monuments of Ādinātha.
34. Aśoka and Īśvara: The Palace, Verse 106, Number 34. During the reign of Aśoka, there were two palaces named Aśoka and Īśvara. Their etymologies are as follows: [text continues].
He in whom sorrow and anger do not exist is Aśoka.
According to Amara, "manyu" and "śoka," however, are feminine when used with the suffix *śuk*.
He whose nature is to rule, whose attribute is sovereignty, and who performs ruling well, is Īśvara.
"Such are the two temples known as Aśokeśvara," meaning the two shrines of the deity;
for Amara states that "harmya" and the like are the residences of the wealthy, while "prāsāda" refers to the palaces of gods and kings.
By this very King Aśoka previously described, in the region called Vijayeśvara, which is famous in this district—
Having constructed a stone wall, two palaces bearing the names described were built in that very location of the assembly hall;

for at that time, whoever beheld that palace called Īśvara was instantly freed from sorrow by the wonder of its excellence in captivating beauty, and thus its name "Aśoka" (Sorrowless) appeared to be truly significant.

Furthermore, since this second temple has attained renown even by the name of the Lord— who possesses the power to act, to refrain from acting, or to act otherwise— it appears that it too has indeed attained its meaningfulness.
Because both of these temples are of such extreme antiquity, there are also certain signs and marks of their construction.
Since it does not exist, no names or other such details spoken by people in the Kashmiri language in modern times have been written here;
however, that which Paṇḍita Kalhaṇa composed in the assembly hall near Vijayeśvara [has been included].
There are two palaces named Śāntāvasāda and Aśokeśvara.
By writing "ityādi" (and so forth), these two palaces are obtained by this very [text]; otherwise, no mention of them is found anywhere—may there be auspiciousness!
